verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel. Here is the hinge of the whole opening argument, and everything from verse 18 to the end of chapter 2 unfolds from it. But first, the half of the verse that sounds wrong. At the end of Matthew’s Gospel the risen Christ sent his apostles out with precisely that instruction: make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Paul was an apostle. How can he say he was not sent to do the very thing the apostles were sent to do?

What he cannot mean. Paul was not against baptism. He was baptised himself as soon as his sight returned (Acts 9:18); he has just named the people he baptised in Corinth (vv. 14–16); he assumes every Corinthian was baptised into Christ’s name (v. 13); and his teaching on what baptism signifies, union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4), is among the richest in the New Testament. Whatever this sentence means, it cannot mean that baptism is optional. Anyone who uses it that way has to explain why Paul baptised anyone at all.

Not this but that. The shape of the sentence is a Hebrew way of stressing priority: not this but that, meaning that first. God says through Hosea, I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6), though it was the same God who had commanded the sacrifices, and the next line shows the comparison: the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. Paul is telling the Corinthians what his commission was chiefly for. Christ sent him to preach (euangelizō, to announce good news). Baptising was not the centre of the assignment, and it did not need an apostle’s hands.

The Great Commission was given to the church. In Matthew’s Greek there is a single command, make disciples; going, baptising and teaching describe how it is carried out. It was given to the eleven as the foundation of the whole church (Matthew 28:16), and the church has obeyed it together, never on the assumption that each apostle had to perform every part in person. Jesus set that pattern himself: John notes that Jesus himself did not baptise, but only his disciples (John 4:2). At Caesarea Peter preached, and then commanded them to be baptised (Acts 10:48). Paul describes the same division of labour two chapters later: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (3:6).

Paul’s particular commission. The risen Christ appointed him a servant and witness and sent him to the Gentiles to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light (Acts 26:16–18); God revealed his Son to him in order that he might preach him among the Gentiles (Galatians 1:16). Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel (9:16). He was a planter of churches, and the preaching was the part only he had been sent to do. Luke records that in Corinth many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptised (Acts 18:8), and does not say by whose hand. So Paul is not contradicting Matthew 28; he is describing his place in obeying it. Disciples are made first by the announcement of Christ crucified, and baptism follows faith, as it did at Pentecost, where those who received his word were baptised (Acts 2:41).

Does it matter who baptised me? It does not. A baptism does not take its value from the reputation of the minister, from how well you knew him, or from whether he later disgraced himself. You were baptised, as every Corinthian was, into the name of Christ (v. 13), and that name is the whole of it.

And not with words of eloquent wisdom. Now the second half of the verse, where the weight of the argument falls. “Eloquent wisdom” is literally wisdom of word (sophia logou): clever rhetoric and human philosophy. In Corinth that phrase had a precise cultural meaning. Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators, the sophists, were celebrities, paid for their performances and judged by their style. Audiences compared them, took sides and attached themselves to a favourite. Rhetoric was competitive entertainment, and the Corinthians wanted their preachers to be impressive. To preach the cross in that register is to enter the competition, and the moment you do, the audience begins assessing the performer. They may leave impressed. They will not leave undone.

Lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. The verb is kenoō: to be emptied, drained, made void. It is the same root as the great word in Philippians 2:7, where the Son emptied himself and took the form of a servant. There it describes a glorious self-emptying; here it describes a disastrous one. The cross can be hollowed out, not by attack but by presentation. A preacher can leave every doctrine formally intact and still drain the thing of power, simply by making the message a vehicle for the messenger. If the preacher dazzles, people believe because of the performance, and the cross’s own power is hidden. The power is in the message of the crucified Christ, not in the messenger.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should be careless or dull, or that learning and clear speech are bad. This verse has been used to defend laziness for centuries. Paul himself argued and reasoned (Acts 17:2; 19:8); he was trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), quotes Greek poets, and constructs arguments in this very letter of considerable sophistication. The man who wrote chapter 13 plainly took enormous trouble over words. A sermon that is muddled, dull and badly prepared is not thereby more spiritual; it is merely worse. It means preachers must not rely on technique or try to make the gospel attractive by hiding its offence.

Two powers. What Paul is against is the substitution of one power for another. Two things can produce a response to preaching: the persuasive skill of the speaker, and the Spirit of God working through the message of a crucified Saviour. Both produce visible results. Only one produces conversions. And the first is easier to obtain, quicker to measure and immediately rewarded, which is why every generation of preachers has to be warned about it. The church that gathers around a preacher’s gifts rather than around the crucified Christ has already begun to drift, however sound its doctrine remains on paper. A herald is a man carrying a message that does not belong to him. The moment the herald becomes interesting in his own right, the message has a rival.

Not for preachers only. Every Christian who has ever tried to explain the faith to someone has felt the same pull in miniature. You are with a colleague or a relative, and the conversation turns; and somewhere underneath the desire for them to see Christ there is a second desire: not to look foolish, to have a good answer ready, to come out of it well. That second desire is exactly what this verse is about, and it is the reason so many of our conversations about Christ are careful, clever and curiously ineffective.

How can I tell whether I am moved by the preacher or by Christ? Ask what you take home. If on Monday you remember chiefly how good the sermon was, the turn of phrase, the story, the cleverness, the preacher may have become the subject. If you remember Christ, what he has done, what he asks of you, and find yourself praying about it, the message has done its work. Another sign is what happens when the gifted preacher is away: if you stay home, you were following him. None of this means you should prefer dull preaching. It means you should pray for your pastor to be clear, and pray for yourself to listen for the Lord behind the voice.

In a sentence. For Christ did not send Paul to baptise, but to preach the gospel, and not with wisdom and eloquence, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, do not worry about being impressive. Speak simply about Christ crucified; the power is in the message. And run this test on any conversation about your faith you have had in the last month. Afterwards, what did you replay in your mind? If it was chiefly your own performance, the point you made well, the thing you wish you had said better, whether they thought you were reasonable, then you know which power you were relying on. The one who has genuinely proclaimed the cross tends to walk away thinking about the other person, because he was never the subject.

For worship. God has arranged it this way on purpose. He could have chosen a method that rewarded eloquence, and the gospel would have travelled through the ancient world on the strength of its orators. Instead he chose a message that no amount of skill can make respectable, a crucified man, so that when it saves anybody at all there is no possibility of mistaking whose power did it. The weakness is not a defect in the method. It is the method. And the crucified Lord at its centre needs no polish from us, because he is himself the power of God, and his cross has never once been emptied by anything but our attempts to improve it.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized polished rhetoric; travelling orators were admired like celebrities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message of the cross seems foolish to those who are perishing, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Scripture foretold that God would confound the wisdom of the wise. Where are the sages, the scholars and the debaters now? God has made the world’s wisdom look foolish. Since the world in its wisdom did not come to know God, God was pleased to save believers through the apparent foolishness of preaching. Jews want miraculous signs and Greeks want wisdom, but Paul preaches a crucified Messiah, an offence to Jews and nonsense to Gentiles, yet to those God calls, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is God’s power and God’s wisdom. God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and his weakness stronger than human strength.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross (Theologia Crucis)

Luther’s distinction between the theology of the cross and the theology of glory is nowhere more clearly grounded than in 1:18–25. The theologian of glory sees God in power, success, and wisdom that makes sense on human terms. The theologian of the cross sees God revealed precisely in weakness, foolishness, and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross is not the means to something better; it is the place where God is most fully known. The cross was never Plan B after the fall. It was the plan from eternity — the place where the justice and the love of God were both satisfied at the same moment, in the same event, in the same Person.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul wrote into a culture where crucifixion was the ultimate symbol of shame, defeat, and criminal status. To preach a crucified Messiah was not merely theologically offensive but socially disqualifying. The early Christians were not brave about something trivial; they were staking their social standing and their lives on an executed criminal. Now: The pressure to make the gospel more palatable — to lead with Jesus-as-life-coach rather than Jesus-as-sin-bearer, to emphasise personal fulfilment rather than atonement — is the contemporary version of Paul’s Corinthian problem. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age. The answer is still to preach it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”

For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing. “The word of the cross” (ho logos tou staurou) is not the cross considered as an event, but the message about it, spoken out loud by somebody: the message that God saves through a crucified man. Paul locates the power in the proclamation, which is why the previous verse mattered so much. God has chosen to save people through an announcement, and the announcement is about an execution. The word for folly is mōria, the root behind our word moron. Paul is not softening it. To the perishing, the cross is not merely unconvincing; it is idiotic, the sort of thing an intelligent person is embarrassed to be associated with. And he says it without defensiveness, because he expects it. A message that the natural mind found reasonable would not be this message.

But to us who are being saved it is the power of God. Two present participles, and English translations rightly keep them moving: those who are perishing (apollymenoi), on the way to destruction, and us who are being saved. Neither is a finished state. Paul is describing two directions of travel, two populations in motion, and the same sentence lands differently depending on which road you are on. The message does not change; the hearers are not in the same condition. And notice that the cross is not merely a message about power; it is God’s power at work, saving people (Romans 1:16). The same message divides humanity into two groups.

When your family thinks it is beneath you. Many readers will recognise this. You have a brother, or a daughter at university, or a colleague at the next desk, who thinks your faith is beneath you. Not hostile, necessarily; often worse than hostile: kind, and faintly embarrassed on your behalf. They can produce the standard objections, and they leave you with the impression that you are a reasonably intelligent person who has made one inexplicable exception. This verse tells you three things about that experience, and you need all three. First, it is predicted. You have not stumbled into an unexpected weakness in Christianity; you have run into precisely what Paul said would happen. Second, the issue is not that you have failed to explain it well. Paul was better at explaining than you are, and the folly verdict came in anyway. Third, and this changes how you pray, the difference between the two responses is not intelligence. Both groups hear the same words; what separates them is which road they are on, and that is God’s business, not yours.

For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart”. The quotation is from Isaiah 29:14, and its background repays a moment. It comes from a passage about people whose religion had become mouth-work, people who drew near with their mouth and honoured God with their lips while their hearts were far from him, and about the wise men of Judah who thought they could manage the Assyrian crisis by clever alliances instead of relying on God. God promised to bring their wisdom to nothing, and he did it by acting in a way none of their calculations had allowed for. Their wisdom perished, not because it was outargued, but because God did something outside its categories. The same happens with every human wisdom that rejects the cross.

God has done this before. The cross completes a pattern. He promised Abraham a son at seventy-five and gave him one at a hundred, with Sarah ninety; he took Israel out of Egypt with no army; he brought them home from Babylon by the decree of a pagan king. Every time, the experts had already established that it could not be done, and every time they were right on their own terms and wrong about the world they were living in (Isaiah 55:8–9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is irrational or that Christians should despise thinking. Paul is not saying that stupidity is holy, or that Christians should be glad to sound ridiculous, or that any objection can be waved away with a verse about the natural man. That is a lazy misuse, and this letter is itself a sustained piece of careful argument. The foolishness is in the content, a crucified Saviour, not in the manner of the people who believe it. We are to be always ready to give a reason (1 Peter 3:15). We are simply told not to be shocked when the reason is found absurd. Human wisdom, as a way to know and reach God, fails; only God’s revelation can save.

Does “being saved” mean I am not saved yet? You are saved, you are being saved, and you will be saved, and all three are true at once. The moment you trusted Christ you were justified, forgiven and adopted, and that can never be undone (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8). Now God is working that salvation out in you, freeing you from sin’s power day by day (Philippians 2:12–13). And at Christ’s return he will complete it, raising your body and removing sin altogether (Romans 13:11; 1 Peter 1:5). Paul uses the present tense here because salvation is begun and continuing, to be completed at Christ’s return. It is not uncertain. It is unfinished, and the one who began it will finish it.

In a sentence. For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.”

On a Tuesday. Next time someone you love treats your faith as an embarrassing exception, do not be rattled and do not be defensive. Answer as well as you can, kindly and without heat. Then pray for him, because what he needs is not a cleverer you but an opened eye, and only God opens eyes.

For worship. If the cross is precious to you and not foolish, that is because God has saved you. You did not see it because you were wiser than your brother. You saw it because the power of God reached you through a message about a dying man, and turned your folly into faith. That same cross that the world laughs at is the place where the Son of God bore the wrath we deserved, and it has been saving people who once laughed at it for two thousand years. Praise him for opening your eyes.

parallels.desc: the wisdom of their wise men shall perish

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.

Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Three questions, and each names a recognised professional. The wise (sophos): the Greek philosopher, the man with an account of reality. The scribe (grammateus): the Jewish scholar of the law, master of the sacred text. The debater of this age (syzētētēs): the professional arguer of the lecture hall, a man who could take either side and win. Between them they represent every avenue by which the ancient world thought truth might be reached: reason, expert handling of revelation, and rhetoric. Where are they? Their wisdom could not save.

The taunt after the battle. The form of the questions is borrowed. Isaiah taunted Egypt in exactly this way: where then are your wise men? (Isaiah 19:12). And again after Jerusalem’s deliverance: where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? (Isaiah 33:18). It is the language of a battlefield after the fact, when the confident men who explained beforehand why it would go the other way are nowhere to be found.

Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? By the cross, God showed that all human wisdom was foolish in the matter of knowing him. He did not argue with it. He simply did what it said could not be done, and left it standing in the empty field.

For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom. This is one of the most compressed and profound sentences Paul ever wrote. Read it slowly, because it contains two different wisdoms and everything turns on keeping them apart. It was God’s wisdom that arranged matters so that human wisdom, with all its philosophy and religion, would not be able to find him (Romans 1:21–22). The failure is not an accident that God then worked around. It is the design, deliberate, so that salvation would be by grace.

Why would God arrange such a thing? Not because knowledge of him is unavailable. Paul argues elsewhere that the creation broadcasts it continuously, so plainly that nobody is left with an excuse (Romans 1:19–20). The barrier was never a shortage of evidence. It is that the mind doing the looking is not neutral. Human beings do not merely fail to find God; they suppress what they find, because the God who is actually there is not one we would have chosen, and he does not leave us in charge. The problem is moral before it is intellectual, which is why more information has never yet converted anybody.

It pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe. So God closed the route that would have let the clever arrive first, and opened one that anybody can walk. “It pleased God” (eudokēsen): it was his good pleasure, his delight. “What we preach” (kērygma) is the content of the message, not just the act of preaching. Paul does not say God saves through folly; he says God saves through the folly of what we preach, the message the world files under nonsense. God chose a message that seems foolish, and a means, preaching, that seems weak. The instrument is preaching. The condition is believing. Not those who are clever, but those who believe. Neither requires a degree.

A mercy with a wide reach. If God had appointed philosophy as the road to himself, the entrance requirements would have excluded almost the whole human race: every illiterate believer in history, everyone without the leisure to think for a living, the woman running a household on no sleep, the man whose schooling ended at fourteen. Instead the requirement is to hear and to trust, and on that basis a professor and a child stand at exactly the same distance from the door.

What it does not mean. It does not mean general revelation is worthless. Creation shows God’s power and divine nature (Romans 1:20). But it cannot bring saving knowledge; only the gospel can.

Then what about people who never hear the gospel? Scripture is plain that salvation comes through conscious faith in Christ, and faith comes by hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:13–17; Acts 4:12). Creation and conscience leave everyone without excuse, but they cannot tell anyone that God has given his Son for sinners (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16). That is why this verse is a missionary verse: it pleased God to save through preaching, so the church must send preachers. We do not need to be anxious that God is unjust; the Judge of all the earth will do right, and those who perish are judged for the light they had and rejected. Infants who die in infancy are in a different case: we hold that elect infants are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3).

In a sentence. Where is the wise person? Where is the teacher of the law? Where is the philosopher of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to be clever to be saved, only to believe, and you do not need to be clever to share it. If you have ever felt intellectually outmatched in a conversation about faith, ask what would actually change if you won the argument. Suppose you had every answer ready and your friend conceded every point. Would he then be a Christian? The evidence of two thousand years is that he would not, because nobody has ever been merely argued into the kingdom; where an argument was involved, God was doing something underneath it. Answer the questions honestly, and take the trouble to answer them well. But do not mistake the argument for the power. The power is in the announcement, and it is God’s to apply.

For worship. It pleased God. Of all the ways he could have saved, he delighted in the one that leaves no one out for lack of brains or breeding, and no one in because of them. The philosopher’s lamp and the scribe’s scroll went out in the dark, and God lit the world with a message about a cross. There is a wisdom deeper than every school and older than every library, and it planned from eternity to save fools like us by the foolishness of a crucified King.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

For Jews demand signs. Two cultures, two currencies, and the cross is legal tender in neither. Many Jews wanted miraculous proofs of power before they would believe, like the wonders of the Exodus (Matthew 12:38; John 6:30). The demand was not unreasonable on its own terms. God had authenticated Moses with plagues and Elijah with fire from heaven; Scripture itself had trained them to expect that when God acts decisively, he shows his hand. What they were waiting for was a powerful Messiah who would do something visible about Rome.

And Greeks seek wisdom. Greeks wanted a philosophy that satisfied the mind and was elegantly argued: a coherent account of the world, beautifully presented.

But we preach Christ crucified. Paul gives neither. He preaches a crucified Messiah. The verb is present: he kept doing it. He did not lead with the resurrection to soften the entrance, and he did not translate the cross into something more presentable. He went into the most status-obsessed city in Greece and announced an executed criminal. And “crucified” is a perfect participle: the one who was crucified and remains the crucified one. The cross is the heart of the message, not an embarrassing detail.

A stumbling block to Jews. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels. For Jews it also meant being under God’s curse, for a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). A crucified Messiah was not merely a failed one; by the plain reading of their own law he was a man under God’s curse, a contradiction in terms. That is why Paul uses the word skandalon, scandal: not an intellectual objection, but a stumbling block, something you trip over and go down.

And folly to Gentiles. The Greek objection was different and just as total. Crucifixion was not a subject for polite society; Cicero said the very word cross should be kept far from a Roman citizen’s thoughts, eyes and ears. To Greeks and Romans, worshipping a crucified Jew was madness, not merely false but tasteless, a category error too grotesque to merit a rebuttal. One of the earliest surviving pictures of the crucifixion is a mocking graffito scratched on a wall in Rome, showing a man worshipping a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, and the caption: Alexamenos worships his god.

But to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks. Then the hinge of the sentence. Not to those who worked it out. Not to those who were open-minded, or better educated, or more spiritually sensitive. Called. The called are those effectively summoned by God, not just invited. You can see the difference in the verse itself. The same Christ crucified is preached to everybody in Corinth. To some he is a stumbling block, to others nonsense, and to a third group the identical message is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Nothing about the sermon changed. What changed was that God called them. The same message is heard by many; to the called, it is life.

Where Christians differ: the general call and the effectual call. Some think that God’s call is only an invitation, which people accept or reject by their own power. Verdict: the gospel is offered to all who hear it, genuinely offered, and all are commanded to believe (the general call). But Paul here speaks of those who are called as distinct from the rest who hear and stumble. This is the effectual call, God’s inward work by the Spirit that makes the gospel powerful in the elect, so that they come freely (Romans 8:30; Westminster 10.1). The first can be refused, and constantly is. The second is God doing in a man what the man could not do in himself. The difference between those who believe and those who mock is God’s calling, not human cleverness.

Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. The cross does not abolish the Jewish hunger for power or the Greek hunger for wisdom; it satisfies both, in the last place either would have looked. They wanted power: here is the true power of God that saves, in a man too weak to carry his own crossbeam (Mark 15:21). They wanted wisdom: here is the wisdom of God that planned salvation, in an event that looks like the collapse of every plan. The categories were not wrong. They were pointed in the wrong direction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean signs and arguments are always bad. Jesus did signs, and Paul reasoned. It means that the cross must stay at the centre, and neither signs nor arguments can replace it.

If only the called believe, why should I evangelise or pray? Because the call comes through the preaching. God does not call people in a vacuum; he calls them through the message of Christ crucified, spoken by ordinary believers (Romans 10:14–17). The effectual call is not a reason to stay silent but the reason to speak with hope: you do not have to produce faith in anyone, and you cannot, but God can, and he has chosen to do it through words like yours. So pray, because the calling is his; and speak, because the calling comes by the word. Without the effectual call, evangelism would be hopeless. With it, no one is beyond reach.

In a sentence. Jews demand signs and Greeks look for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those whom God has called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Notice the version of Christ you are most tempted to offer people: the one who makes life work, the one who answers every intellectual puzzle, the one who will improve their family. All may be true in their place. But the Christ who saves is the Christ crucified, and if your friend never hears about the cross from you, he has not yet heard the part that has power. Find a natural way this week to say why Jesus died.

For worship. Consider what he did. He could have come with the signs they demanded; he had done greater things with a word, and twelve legions of angels were available for the asking (Matthew 26:53). He could have come with the wisdom they sought, and held the lecture halls of Athens spellbound for forty years. He chose instead the one form of death designed to make a man contemptible, and went to it deliberately, in public, outside a city wall, between two criminals, for people who were at that moment shouting for it. The Jews asked for a sign and were given the only one that could save them. The Greeks asked for wisdom and were handed the wisdom of God with nails through it. There has never been a moment in the history of the universe when God looked less like God, or was more fully himself (Colossians 2:14–15).
verseByVerse.note: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, reserved for slaves and rebels; for Jews, a crucified man was under God’s curse.

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.

For the foolishness of God is wiser than men. Read flatly, the sentence is close to blasphemy, and Paul knows exactly what he is doing. God has no foolishness and no weakness. Paul speaks ironically, from inside the world’s verdict. Very well: you have looked at the cross and filed it under folly and weakness. Take your own categories, then, and follow them where they lead. What looks like foolishness on God’s part, saving through a crucified man, is wiser than all human wisdom combined. He does not argue the verdict. He accepts it provisionally and explodes it from within.

The comparison is not close. Set the cross against the accumulated wisdom of the human race, every philosophy, every ethical system, every scheme for making people good, and ask which of them has actually dealt with guilt. Not managed it, or explained it away, or advised us to be gentler with ourselves. Dealt with it. The wisest thing the world has ever devised leaves a man exactly where he was, with his record and his conscience intact and no remedy for either. What the world calls foolish removed the record.

And the weakness of God is stronger than men. The cross looked like weakness: the Son of God helpless, mocked, dying. Rome had the most efficient machinery of force the ancient world had seen, and it was employed that Friday to its full effect, and it worked: the man died. Three days later the thing that machinery existed to prevent had happened anyway, and within three centuries the empire that ran the machinery was bowing to the name of the victim. By the cross God defeated sin, death and Satan (Colossians 2:15). Whatever was operating in that tomb was not weakness with a good result. It was strength of a kind the categories had no room for. When God looks weak, he is often about to do something the universe has never seen. Good Friday looked like the defeat of everything. Easter Sunday answered the question.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is actually foolish or weak. Paul is speaking from the world’s viewpoint.

Into your own weakness. This is the verse to take into your own weakness, which is where most readers will need it. There is a persistent assumption in us that God works through our strong points: that he will use the areas where we are competent and impressive, and that our weaknesses are the parts of us he has to work around. This verse says the opposite about him, and Paul will later say the opposite about himself: it was in his weakness that Christ’s power rested on him, which is why he stopped asking for the thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

So should I not bother developing my abilities? No. Your abilities are gifts from God, and you should develop them and use them gladly (Matthew 25:14–30). The point is where you put your trust. Strength used in dependence on God is a tool in his hand; strength trusted in instead of God is an idol, and he will often break it. And weakness is not a virtue in itself; it is the place where we stop pretending and lean on him, which is why he does so much there. Work hard, and pray as one who knows the results are his.

In a sentence. For the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom, and the weakness of God is stronger than human strength.

On a Tuesday. When God’s ways look foolish or weak in your situation, remember the cross. His weakness wins. Then make two lists: the things about your life you would put forward as useful to God, and the things you have long regarded as disqualifying: the failure, the illness, the temperament, the years you cannot get back, the thing you are ashamed of. Ask which list looks more like a cross. The pattern of this verse is not that God tolerates the second list. It is that the second list is where he has often done his most significant work, and the first is where we are most likely to get in his way.

For worship. He saves by dying. He reigns from a cross. He conquers by being conquered. Every one of those sentences is nonsense by the world’s arithmetic, which is precisely why the world’s arithmetic has never once produced a resurrection. The wisest minds in history never found a way to take away one sin; the Son of God, hanging helpless, took away the sin of the world. Blessed be the God whose foolishness outthinks us and whose weakness overcomes the grave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to look at their own church. Not many of them were clever, powerful or well-born by worldly standards. God deliberately chose what the world thinks foolish, weak, low and contemptible, even what counts for nothing, to put the proud and the important to shame, so that no human being can boast before him. It is God who has placed them in Christ Jesus, and Christ has become for them wisdom from God: their righteousness, their holiness and their redemption. So, as Scripture says, anyone who boasts should boast in the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Doctrine of Boasting: Sola Gratia Applied

The logic of vv. 28–29 is the logic of grace pushed to its social conclusion: God chooses the things that are “not” to bring to nothing the things that “are” — “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” This is the pastoral and sociological outworking of sola gratia. If salvation were partly dependent on human wisdom, power, or birth, then at least some people could boast. But when God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors, and the socially marginal, the only conceivable boast is in the grace that did what human merit could never have achieved. God’s choosing of the lowly things is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness but a deliberate demolition of every ground of human pride before him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social hierarchy was steep and rigid: Roman citizens over freedpersons over slaves; the educated over the illiterate; patrons over clients. The church at Corinth crossed every one of these lines — and the crossing was theological, not merely sociological. It was evidence of the same gospel that the cross proclaimed. Now: The church that unconsciously mirrors the class and status structures of its surrounding culture is denying with its sociology what it affirms with its theology. The cross creates a community where the only legitimate boast is in the Lord — which means no other boast is legitimate at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;

For consider your calling, brothers. “Consider” (blepete): look at it. Paul has been arguing the point theologically for eight verses; now he tells them to check it against the evidence in the room. Look at yourselves. Look at who was in the church when God called you. The proof of everything he has said about God’s method is sitting in their own congregation.

Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. Literally, according to the flesh. The three terms are the standard triad of ancient status: education, influence and birth. Those were the things that determined where you sat, who returned your greeting, and what your life would be. Most of the Corinthian believers were not educated, influential or high-born. Many were slaves, freedmen and workers. Paul’s observation is simply demographic: look at who has actually been converted here.

Not many, not none. Note the precision. He does not say none, and the church at Corinth proves that too: Crispus the synagogue ruler, Gaius who was host to the whole church, and Erastus the city treasurer (Romans 16:23), a man holding public office. The gospel is not a movement of the poor that excludes the comfortable; God saves treasurers as well as slaves. But they were the exceptions, and everybody in the room knew it.

What the critics said. The outside world certainly knew it. More than a century later the pagan critic Celsus was still sneering that Christianity was a religion of wool-workers, cobblers and laundry-workers, who would say nothing in front of educated men but got hold of children and women in back rooms. He meant it as a demolition. He was describing, with reasonable accuracy, what Paul says here God did on purpose.

But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise. “Chose” (eklegomai) comes three times in verses 27–28. God’s choice was deliberate. He passed by the people the world admires and chose the people it overlooks. And the purpose is stated: to shame the wise.

God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong. “Shame” (kataischynō): put to shame, disgrace. Not to bypass the strong, nor merely to show he could manage without them, but to shame them, and the shaming happens by the simple fact of the outcome. By saving the weak, God shows that salvation has nothing to do with human strength. When the people who could not have found God by wisdom are manifestly full of God, the whole apparatus of wisdom stands exposed as useless for the one thing that finally mattered.

For the ordinary Christian. There is a particular kind of Christian who reads a chapter like this and feels quietly outside it. You are not a leader. You have no platform and no obvious gift. You did not do well at school, or your career went nowhere, or your life has been spent on work nobody records, and somewhere in you is the settled belief that you are one of the ordinary ones, that the real work of God is done by other people, and that your part is to make up the numbers and be grateful. Read the verse again. That is not a description of your limitations. It is a description of God’s preference. He did not accept the unimpressive because nobody better applied. He chose them, and he chose them for a reason that has nothing to do with their inadequacy and everything to do with what he intends to show.

Not a new policy. He picked a childless couple to found a nation, a shepherd boy over seven older brothers, a man slow of speech to confront Pharaoh, and a young woman in a village nobody respected to carry the Son of God. When he wanted twelve men to take the gospel to the whole world he passed over the religious establishment of Jerusalem and took fishermen off a beach. The pattern is so consistent that the surprising thing would be if he had chosen otherwise (1 Samuel 16:7; Luke 1:52; Matthew 11:25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never saves the wise or wealthy, or that poverty earns salvation. It means God does not choose people because of their worldly advantages.

Should the church then not bother reaching the educated and influential? It should reach everyone, and Paul himself reasoned with philosophers in Athens and spoke before governors and kings (Acts 17:22–31; 26:1–29). Not many is not none, and the gospel is for the powerful as much as the poor. What this verse forbids is courting people because of their status, giving the rich man the good seat (James 2:1–4), or thinking the church will be strengthened chiefly by attracting impressive people. A church that only seeks the influential has forgotten how it began. Reach everyone, honour everyone, and expect God to fill his house mostly with people the world overlooks.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, think of what you were when you were called. Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were influential; not many were of noble birth. But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong.

On a Tuesday. Think of what you would need to become before you would consider yourself genuinely useful to God: more articulate, more confident, better taught, further on. Now notice that you have just described a kind of person God has repeatedly declined to rely on. The qualification he looks for is not on that list at all. Offer him what you are this week, and see what he does with it.

For worship. If you are not impressive by the world’s standards, rejoice: God chose you. If you are, rejoice too, but know that your advantages had nothing to do with it. Look around the room next Sunday and see the evidence of his heart: the God who stooped to a stable, who touched lepers and ate with outcasts, has filled his house with people like us, and he is not embarrassed by his family. He is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.

God chose what is low and despised in the world. Paul is building to a climax and the language intensifies. Not merely the foolish and the weak now, but the low (agenē, without family, of no birth) and the despised (exouthenēmena, treated as nothing).

Even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are. Then a phrase that goes past every social category: ta mē onta, the things that do not exist. He means the people who do not register. Not the poor, who at least appear in a census; the ones who make no impression at all, whose names are on no list, whose absence would alter nothing, who are, as far as the world’s accounting goes, simply not there. In a Roman colony obsessed with rank this was not a metaphor: a slave had almost no legal personality. Paul reaches for the strongest word available and says: those are the ones God chose. Things that are not are the nobodies; things that are are the somebodies. God uses nobodies to nullify (katargeō) the somebodies.

God’s signature. The phrase is not chosen at random, because it is God’s signature. He is the God who calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17). He made the universe out of nothing at all. So when he builds a church out of nobodies, he is not making the best of poor material; he is doing what he has always done, in the way he has always done it. Creation out of nothing is not an emergency measure. It is his ordinary method.

So that no human being might boast in the presence of God. The purpose is stated without softening, and it is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking towards. “No human being” is literally no flesh. This is the purpose of election. If God had chosen people for their wisdom, power or birth, they could boast. If he saved by achievement, effort or sincerity, in every case somebody would arrive with a contribution and a reason to be pleased with himself. By choosing nobodies, he excludes all boasting (Romans 3:27; Ephesians 2:8–9). He has closed every one of those doors, not because he dislikes achievement, but because a saved man boasting in the presence of God would be a lie about what happened, and God will not build his kingdom on a lie.

Grace pressed to its social conclusion. It is not merely that boasting is unattractive; it is that boasting has been made impossible by the design of salvation. God’s choosing of the lowly is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness but a deliberate demolition of every ground of human pride before him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God chose people because they were lowly. Lowliness is not merit either. God chose freely, and the lowliness of those chosen displays that freedom.

For the one who feels like a nothing. Some readers do not struggle with pride at all. They struggle with the settled sense of being a nobody: a life that has not amounted to anything, a name nobody would recognise, years that produced nothing anyone could point to. If that is you, this verse is not a general encouragement; it is addressed to you, and it says two things you should not miss. First, God knows the category exists and did not look away from it. He did not choose people despite their being nothing, as if he had to overlook something; the text says the nothings are what he chose. Second, he chose them to bring to nothing things that are. He is not collecting the overlooked in order to keep them safely at the back. He is deploying them to dismantle everything the world has been impressed by. That is not a consolation prize. It is a commission.

If no one may boast, is it wrong to feel pleased with something I have done well? No. Paul himself rejoices over the work God did through him (15:10; 2 Corinthians 1:12). There is a right gladness in work well done, a child well raised, a kindness that landed. The difference is where the credit goes. Boasting before God treats the thing as my ground of standing, my reason to be accepted, my proof that I am better than others. Gratitude receives it as his gift, worked through me, and gives him the praise. A simple check: can you rejoice just as much when God does the same through someone else? If so, you are probably giving thanks, not boasting.

In a sentence. God chose the lowly things of this world and the despised things, and the things that are not, to nullify the things that are, so that no one may boast before him.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to feel superior to other Christians, remember: none of us has anything to boast of before God. And complete this sentence honestly: the thing I would most want said about me at my funeral is ______. Then ask whether that thing is on the list God has just declared he is bringing to nothing. Most of us find our deepest ambitions are for exactly the wise, powerful, well-born register that this passage says God passed over, and it is better to know that now, while there is still time to want something else.

For worship. Nobody will boast in his presence. Not the philosopher who explained the universe, not the emperor whose name is on the arch, not the Christian who served for sixty years. When that room is finally full, there will be one figure in it who is not there by grace, and every voice will be occupied with him: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:11–13). The God who spoke light out of nothing has spoken a church out of nobodies, and the whole of it will sing his praise for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,

And because of him you are in Christ Jesus. “Because of him” is literally from him (ex autou): God is the source of your being in Christ. Not because you found him. Not because you were searching and happened to look in the right place. Union with Christ is God’s work, not yours, and every one of the four gifts that follow arrives by that route.

Who became to us wisdom from God. Then Paul says something he says nowhere else in quite this way. He does not write that Christ gives us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. He writes that Christ became them to us. These are not commodities dispensed from a distance by a generous benefactor. They are a Person, handed over. You do not receive four parcels; you receive him, and he turns out to be all four.

The end of shopping. That distinction is the cure for Corinth. They were shopping: wisdom from Apollos, status from their gifts, standing from their faction. Paul’s answer is not that they were shopping in the wrong places but that the shopping was over before it began. Everything they were assembling piecemeal was already theirs in one Person.

Wisdom. The city was full of it for sale, and the Corinthians were paying. Christ himself is our wisdom. They were seeking wisdom; it was standing in front of them, in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). That does not mean a Christian knows more about everything. It means he knows the one thing on which everything else finally depends: who God is, and how a guilty man may stand before him. No philosopher in history worked that out. Paul then explains what this wisdom consists of, in three words.

Righteousness. This is the great Reformation word, and it must be plain. Christ is our right standing before God. His righteousness is counted to us: justification (Romans 3:22; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). It does not mean God has made you a good person and now accepts you. It means that in Christ you are counted right with God, his record credited to you, your record charged to him. Luther called it an alien righteousness: not produced in you, but reckoned to you, and therefore not subject to how your week has gone. It answers the question underneath all religion: how can I possibly be right with God? You cannot. He became it for you.

Where Christians differ: imputed righteousness. Some deny that Christ’s righteousness is counted to believers, saying instead that God makes us righteous inwardly, and accepts us on that basis. Verdict: Christ became our righteousness. Our right standing with God is not our own inner goodness but Christ’s obedience counted to us, received by faith alone (Romans 4:5–6; 5:19). Sanctification, which follows, is the inward renewal; it is distinct from justification but never separated from it. Both are found in Christ, so the one who has Christ has both.

And sanctification. Christ is our holiness. The same word appeared in verse 2, and it is doing the same work. In him we are set apart for God, before ever we begin to grow holier, and from him we receive the Spirit who makes us holy. That is why this letter can call the Corinthians sanctified while telling them to stop visiting prostitutes (6:15–20). The status comes first and the change follows from it; a Christian does not become holy in order to be accepted, but works out a holiness he has already been given.

And redemption. Apolytrōsis: the word for buying a slave out of bondage. Christ is our release, bought by the price of his blood (Ephesians 1:7). It looks back to a price paid, and it looks forward to a deliverance not yet complete, when the body itself is finally free at the resurrection (Romans 8:23). It is the last word of the four because it is the last thing to arrive.

The whole of a Christian’s life. Set them side by side and they cover the whole of a Christian’s existence: wisdom for the mind that could not find God, righteousness for the guilt that could not be removed, sanctification for the life that could not be cleaned, redemption for the body that will not last. Past, present and future, and all four located in one place.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ gives us these things as separate packages to collect. He is them. Have Christ, and you have all of them.

If Christ is my sanctification, do I need to make any effort? Yes, and gladly. Paul tells the same Corinthians to flee sexual immorality, to discipline the body, and to be steadfast and immovable (6:18; 9:27; 15:58). Christ being your holiness does not make you passive; it makes your effort hopeful. You work out your salvation because God is at work in you (Philippians 2:12–13), and the Spirit you received from Christ is the power by which you fight. The difference from religion is the direction: you are not striving to become acceptable, you are striving because you are accepted, and every step of growth is drawn from him. Effort without Christ is self-improvement; Christ without effort is a misunderstanding.

In a sentence. It is because of God that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God, that is, our righteousness, holiness and redemption.

On a Tuesday. Take the thing you are most anxious about tonight: the standing you are trying to establish, the guilt you are still carrying, the change in yourself you have failed to produce, the future you cannot secure. Ask which of the four it belongs to. Then ask why you have been looking for it anywhere other than in him, and take it to him by name.

For worship. He became these things. That is the astonishing verb. He did not send them; he became them, which means the wisdom has a face, and the righteousness has hands with holes in them, and the sanctification was purchased by a man who was himself made sin, and the redemption cost the Redeemer everything he had. There is nothing a soul requires that is not, at this moment, at the right hand of the Father in a body that still bears the marks of what it cost to obtain it. Christ is your wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption. You need nothing more and no one else.

parallels.desc: the LORD is our righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

So that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord”. The chapter ends where it was always going: a quotation, and one adequate boast. Paul is citing Jeremiah 9:24, and it repays looking up, because he has abbreviated it, and the full sentence (Jeremiah 9:23–24) is the whole argument of this chapter written six centuries earlier. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows the LORD.

Wisdom, might, riches. Set that beside verse 26, wise, powerful, of noble birth, and you can see why Paul reached for this text. He has been preaching Jeremiah’s sermon to Corinth. The three grounds of human boasting have not altered in six hundred years, nor in the two thousand since; only the vocabulary moves.

Not stop boasting, but boast in the right thing. Notice what the verse does not say. It does not say: stop boasting. Paul could have written that, and it would have been a lesser thing. The instinct to boast, to have something to point to, some answer to whether your life amounts to anything, is not surgically removed when a person becomes a Christian. It is redirected. The verb kauchaomai covers glorying, exulting, taking pride in, and Paul uses it of himself freely elsewhere (Galatians 6:14). Boasting itself is not wrong; the question is never whether you will glory in something. It is what. And notice what Jeremiah says the right boast consists of: not that you have achieved anything, but that you understand and know the LORD. Even the boast is not about you. It is about being on terms with someone.

The LORD is Jesus. There is one more thing, easy to miss. In Jeremiah the one to be known is the LORD, the covenant name of God, the name later generations would not even pronounce. Paul condenses the whole sentence to boast in the Lord and applies it, without a syllable of explanation, to the crucified man he has been preaching since verse 18. He does not argue for it or flag it as a development. It is simply where the sentence lands: the Lord in whom we boast is the Lord Jesus, Yahweh come in the flesh.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never take joy in anything else. It means our glory, confidence and pride rest in the Lord alone.

What does boasting in the Lord sound like in real life? It sounds like telling people what God has done rather than what you have done: how he found you, how he carried you through the illness, how he answered a prayer, how Christ forgave a sin you thought unforgivable. It sounds like giving the credit away when you are praised, not with false modesty, but with honest thanks. It sounds like speaking of Christ with the same warmth you would use for a person you admire. And on the bad days it sounds like this: I have nothing, but I have him. Boasting in the Lord is not a religious technique. It is what people naturally do about the thing they treasure most.

In a sentence. Therefore, as it is written: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

On a Tuesday. Notice what you boast about today: your work, your children, your church, your opinions. Think of the last time you felt genuinely diminished, overlooked in a conversation, outperformed by someone younger, made to feel small at a family gathering, and notice what your mind reached for to restore itself. Everyone has a reserve, a fact about themselves they return to when their standing feels threatened: a qualification, a competence, a moral comparison, a child doing well, a hardship endured, a theological position more rigorous than the other person’s. That reserve is your boast, whatever you would say in church, and every one of them can be taken from you, usually by nothing more dramatic than time. The boast Jeremiah names cannot. Turn your boasting into boasting in the Lord.

For worship. The chapter that began with people boasting in Paul, in Apollos, in Cephas, in their own eloquence and knowledge and rank, ends by taking every one of those props away and putting a single name in the empty space. Not a system, not a teacher, not a tradition, and not an achievement of ours. A Person, the LORD of Jeremiah come in the flesh, who became wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption for people who had none of the four, and who is worth boasting about for ever, by a church that had nothing whatever to bring him.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me
