Third, with biting irony, Paul contrasts their self-satisfied sense of already reigning with the apostles’ real life: hungry, beaten, homeless, treated as the scum of the world (vv. 8–13). Finally, Paul speaks as their spiritual father. He warns them as beloved children, sends Timothy, and asks whether they want him to come with a rod or with gentle love (vv. 14–21). The cross shapes not only the message but the messenger’s life, and the chapter that begins with servants who own nothing ends by pointing to the Servant who had every right to come with a rod and came to bear it instead.

This is how one should regard us. Paul is issuing a correction to the lens, not to the facts. The Corinthians have the right men in view, Paul, Apollos, Peter, and they are looking at them through the wrong instrument. They had been viewing their teachers the way Corinth viewed its orators and philosophers: as celebrities to be followed, compared and ranked. Paul takes the lens away and hands them another one with two words ground into it, and both are humbling.

As servants of Christ. The first word is hypēretēs, a word with the vocabulary of rowing in its history: the oarsman on the lower bench, pulling under someone else’s command, in a ship whose course he had no part in setting. By Paul’s day it meant any subordinate assistant, the attendant who waits on an official, but the flavour remains. A servant in this sense supplies effort under somebody else’s direction. He does not choose the destination, and nobody on the quay cheers the oarsmen by name. And notice whose servants they are: of Christ. Not of the Corinthians, who were treating their ministers as hired entertainers, and not of a party. A man who rows for Christ cannot also be steering for the people who prefer him.

And stewards of the mysteries of God. The second word is oikonomos, the steward: the household manager, very often a slave, who ran the estate, kept the accounts and dispensed the stores to the rest of the household (Luke 12:42). He handled a great deal of wealth and owned none of it. That is the exact position of a man entrusted with the gospel: real responsibility, considerable trust, and no ownership whatever. What he distributes is not his, and he cannot alter the terms on which it is given out. And what is being administered is the mysteries of God, which in Paul’s vocabulary never means esoteric secrets kept from ordinary people. It means the thing once hidden and now announced: Christ crucified, and the nations brought in (2:7; Ephesians 3:6). A steward of that has one job, which is to hand out what he was given, in the form he was given it, to everyone in the house.

Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful. Then the single criterion. Not gifted. Not effective. Not admired. Faithful (pistos): trustworthy, reliable, loyal to the master, which means simply that the master’s goods arrive where the master intended, unadulterated and undiminished. Notice how completely that displaces every measurement the Corinthians were using. They were ranking their teachers by eloquence and impact. Paul says the only question is whether the man can be trusted with something that is not his. A steward is not assessed by how much the household admired him, but by whether the accounts balance when the master comes home.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers are a priestly class who dispense grace through rituals. The mysteries are the gospel truths, which they proclaim. They are stewards of a message, not keepers of a sacred store that only they can unlock. Nor does it mean gifts and effectiveness are worthless; God gives gifts to be used. It means that none of them is the test.

Is this only about pastors? No. Paul is speaking first of himself and Apollos, but every Christian is a steward of something (1 Peter 4:10). Money, time, a gift, a position, a family, a piece of knowledge somebody trusted you with: all of it is held rather than owned, and the question in each case is the same. The parable of the talents is told to ordinary disciples, and its verdict is not well done, good and successful servant, but good and faithful (Matthew 25:21). So the mother at home with small children, the man in an office no one will ever write about, the elderly saint who can only pray: each is managing the master’s goods, and each will be asked the same single question.

What should I look for in a pastor, then? Look for faithfulness before flair. Does he preach what Scripture actually says, including the parts that are unpopular, or does he edit the stores to suit the household? Does he live what he preaches, at home and in private as well as on the platform (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? Does he point to Christ rather than to himself? Is he the same man in a small meeting as in a large one? A gifted speaker is a gift from God, and you may thank God for one. But a church that chooses or rates its ministers by charisma alone is repeating Corinth’s mistake, and it usually ends up with stewards who own the house.

What if a faithful minister’s church stays small? Then he has not failed. Faithfulness and visible results are not the same thing, and Scripture is full of faithful servants with thin harvests. Noah preached for decades and eight people entered the ark. Jeremiah preached for forty years to a nation that did not listen. Some of the most faithful pastors in history laboured in obscure villages and are known now only to God. Numbers are not unimportant, because God wants his house full, but growth is God’s work (3:6–7), and the steward is responsible only for what is in his hands. Pray for your pastor, and do not measure him by a scale the Lord does not use.

In a sentence. This, then, is how you ought to regard us: as servants of Christ and as those entrusted with the mysteries God has revealed. Now it is required that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful.

On a Tuesday. Whatever God has entrusted to you, your family, your job, your gifts, the one question is: am I faithful with it? Here is a test worth running on whatever you are responsible for. Ask what you would have to change if you genuinely believed it was not yours: the money, the diary, the influence, the platform, the children. Most of us discover we have been quietly behaving as proprietors of an estate we were only ever managing, and that the change required is not in how hard we work but in whose interests we are working (Luke 12:42–44).

For worship. The Master of this household is the only one in it who owns anything, and he is the one who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). Every steward in his house handles riches he did not earn and cannot add to: the mysteries hidden for ages and now opened, Christ crucified for sinners and the nations gathered in. The faithful servant is a man trusted with treasure, and the treasure is the Lord himself. He was faithful over God’s house as a Son (Hebrews 3:6), and he has never once mislaid a single thing his Father gave him (John 6:39).
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a trusted household manager, often a slave, put in charge of his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.

But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. The Corinthians were evaluating their teachers, comparing Paul unfavourably with others. “Judged” is anakrinō: examined, cross-examined, as in a preliminary hearing. And “human court” is literally a human day: a human day of judgment, set against the Day of the Lord that Paul has just described in 3:13. It sounds dismissive, and it is not. Paul is not saying their opinion is worthless; he is saying it is not the verdict. A jury’s view matters enormously until you learn it was never empanelled. The Corinthians had set up a bench, called witnesses, and begun passing sentence on apostles, and Paul simply observes that the court has no jurisdiction.

In fact, I do not even judge myself. Then he goes further than anyone expects. He removes his own assessment from the court as well. Paul does not trust his self-evaluation any more than theirs. That is not low self-esteem; it is accurate self-knowledge. He knows that the examiner and the accused are the same man, and that no man has full access to his own motives.

For I am not aware of anything against myself. Now the most searching admission in the passage. His conscience is clear about his ministry among them: he knows of no unfaithfulness, no doctrine watered down, no money taken, no flattery used. He has examined himself and found nothing.

But I am not thereby acquitted. And he refuses to treat that as a verdict of innocence. “Acquitted” is dedikaiōmai, from dikaioō, the great word of justification, here used in its courtroom sense: declared in the right. Stop on this, because it is one of the most honest sentences Paul ever wrote about self-knowledge. A clear conscience is not the final verdict. Conscience can be wrong, or blind, or badly taught. We are all judges sitting on our own cases, with an interest in the outcome and incomplete evidence. The psalmist knew it when he asked God to do what he could not do for himself: search me, O God, and know my heart (Psalm 139:23–24). Jeremiah knew it when he called the heart deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9): it lies not only to others but to its owner. Paul is not saying his salvation is uncertain. He is saying that his faithfulness as a servant will be assessed by the Lord, not by his own feelings.

It is the Lord who judges me. Christ alone is qualified to evaluate his servants, because he alone sees everything, including the motives Paul cannot see in himself. This is the hinge of the whole passage, and it produces not anxiety but a strange freedom. If the only judge who counts sees everything, then two exhausting occupations become unnecessary. You need not manage your reputation, because the verdict does not depend on what people conclude about you. And you need not run a permanent internal tribunal, because your own assessment was never authoritative either.

If a clear conscience does not acquit me, how can I have any assurance? A guard is needed at once, because this verse can land on an anxious Christian like a sentence. Am I to go through life suspecting myself? No, and the answer is in the same clause. Paul’s point is not that he is secretly condemned but that the verdict is not his to give, in either direction. He refuses to acquit himself and equally refuses to condemn himself. Both are the Lord’s business, and the Lord has already spoken about those who are in Christ: there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Assurance does not rest on the quality of your self-examination. It rests on Christ’s finished work and God’s promise, sealed to you by the Spirit (Romans 8:16). John writes the same comfort to people whose hearts were accusing them: God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything (1 John 3:19–20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers are above accountability or criticism. Elders can be rebuked for sin (1 Timothy 5:19–20), and churches are told to test what they hear (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Paul himself welcomed being checked against Scripture (Acts 17:11). It means the final evaluation of a servant’s faithfulness belongs to Christ, and ministers should not live for human approval. Nor does it mean self-examination is pointless: Paul commands it before the Lord’s Supper (11:28). Examine yourself, by all means; just do not mistake your findings for the Judge’s verdict.

So should I ignore criticism? No: listen to it, but do not bow to it. Criticism is often a gift, and the Lord frequently uses other people to show us what we cannot see (Proverbs 27:6). Ask honestly whether it is true, whether it agrees with Scripture, and whether people who love you are saying the same thing. If it is true, repent and be grateful. If it is false, you may let it go without bitterness, because the person who said it was never your judge. The difference Paul is drawing is between taking criticism seriously and treating it as a verdict. The first is humility. The second is slavery to opinion, and it will leave you either crushed or defensive.

In a sentence. Paul cares very little if he is judged by you or by any human court; indeed, he does not even judge himself. His conscience is clear, but that does not make him innocent. It is the Lord who judges him.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last piece of criticism that stayed with you for days, and the last piece of praise you found yourself replaying. Ask what authority you granted to each. Most of us hand out judicial powers very freely, to a colleague, a relative, an anonymous comment online, and then live under sentences passed by people who were never on the bench. When the voice in your own head starts its familiar hearing, either acquitting you too quickly or condemning you without mercy, you may say to it what Paul said: you are not the judge either. Ask the Lord to search your heart (Psalm 139:23–24). Then rest in his judgment, not in others’ opinions or even your own.

For worship. There is one Judge. He knows everything, including the faithfulness nobody noticed and the sins you have forgotten, and he is the one who died for you. The Lord who will examine his servants is the Lord who was himself cross-examined in a human court, at night, by men with no jurisdiction, and who answered nothing, because he was leaving his case with the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He bore the verdict we deserved, so that the only courtroom which matters holds nothing over us but his name. He is our Judge, and he is our righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God.

Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time. The fault Paul names is not judging as such but the timing of it: a verdict delivered before the evidence is complete and before the Judge has taken his seat. The Corinthians were acting as judges of their ministers before the real judgment day, ranking and rating, settling who was first-class and who was second-rate. Paul tells them to stop, because the court has not yet sat.

Not a ban on all judging. A guard is needed immediately, because this is among the most quoted verses in the modern church, and almost always for the wrong purpose. It is produced to shut down any moral assessment whatever. But the same letter, one chapter later, has Paul pronouncing judgment on a man’s conduct (5:3), instructing the church to judge those inside it (5:12), and asking incredulously whether they are really unable to settle a dispute between brothers (6:5). Whatever this verse forbids, it cannot be the thing Paul does immediately afterwards.

What is reserved. What it forbids is the verdict only God can reach: the assessment of another person’s heart and final standing. You may say that an action is wrong; Scripture requires it. You may not say what a man is before God, or what he was really after, because you do not have the file. That distinction is worth holding onto, because we cross it constantly and casually. It is the difference between “what he said was untrue” and “he is a liar through and through”; between “this decision was unwise” and “he only did it for the credit”. The first is observation. The second is a ruling on the purposes of the heart, and it is reserved.

Before the Lord comes. The time of judgment is the return of Christ. History has an appointed day on which every unsettled question will be settled by the only one who can settle it, and that date is already in the Father’s diary (Acts 17:31). Everything until then is the preliminary hearing.

Who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness. Not necessarily evil things, but everything hidden from human view: everything done in the dark, and the reasons behind everything done in the light. Which is a solemn prospect, and Paul means it to be. There will be no missing evidence and no successful spin. The charitable act done to be noticed, the generosity that was an investment in reputation, the service rendered to secure a position: all of it disclosed. And equally the things nobody ever knew: the kindness done anonymously, the temptation resisted in private, the years of quiet faithfulness in a place where it was never noticed, the prayers no one heard.

And will disclose the purposes of the heart. “Purposes” (boulai) are counsels, motives, the reasons a person acts. Only God sees them. Two ministers may do the same thing, one for Christ’s glory and one for his own, and from the pew they look identical. Two Christians may give the same gift, teach the same class, sing in the same choir. Only the Lord knows which was love and which was performance, and he is the only one entitled to say.

Then each one will receive his commendation from God. Here the verse becomes unexpectedly wonderful. The word is epainos: praise, approval spoken aloud. Read it again slowly. Paul has just said the Day will expose the hidden purposes of every heart, and he expects the outcome for God’s servants to be praise. Not a bare acquittal, not a relieved escape: commendation, from God, to each one. It is the note of the master in the parable saying well done, good and faithful servant (Matthew 25:21), and it is from God that praise matters (Romans 2:29). That God should forgive us is grace beyond calculation. That he should then intend to praise us, having himself supplied everything he is praising, is something else again. Augustine said that when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts. The judgment Christians most instinctively dread is described here as the occasion on which their Father speaks well of them out loud (1 Peter 1:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may never make any judgments now. In the next chapter Paul commands the church to judge a sinning member (5:12), and elsewhere he tells believers to test teaching and to mark those who cause divisions (Romans 16:17). What is forbidden is judging motives, pronouncing on someone’s final standing, and ranking servants of Christ as if we could see their hearts.

Will my sins be exposed in front of everyone on that day? Scripture says plainly that nothing will stay hidden (Luke 12:2–3; 2 Corinthians 5:10), and it does not give us the details of how that disclosure happens. But two things are certain for the believer. First, your sins were already judged, in full, at the cross; whatever is brought to light on that day is brought to light as forgiven, covered by the blood of Christ, and no charge can be laid against God’s elect (Romans 8:33). Second, the emphasis of this very verse is not exposure but commendation. The Day that uncovers everything is, for those in Christ, the Day of their Father’s praise. You need not dread it. You may long for it.

Is it wrong to want God’s praise? No; it is the right ambition, and Paul holds it out to us as a motive. What is wrong is wanting people’s praise instead of God’s (John 12:43), or wanting God’s praise as a wage that puts him in our debt. Jesus told his disciples to do their giving and praying in secret, precisely so that the Father who sees in secret would reward them (Matthew 6:4, 6). Children of a good father want to hear him say “well done”, and he wants to say it. The desire becomes healthy when we remember that every good thing he will praise in us, he first put there.

In a sentence. Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes. He will bring to light what is hidden in darkness and will expose the motives of the heart. At that time each will receive their praise from God.

On a Tuesday. You cannot see other people’s motives. Give them the benefit of the doubt, and leave the heart to God. Catch yourself this week at the moment you move from “that was unkind” to “she is that sort of person”, or from “that seemed showy” to “he only does it to be seen”. Stop at the first sentence. And if you are the one whose motives are being questioned unfairly, whose faithfulness nobody sees, take heart: the Lord who sees in secret has a word of praise prepared, and nobody else’s verdict can cancel it.

For worship. The Lord who will light up every hidden thing is the Light of the world, and he does not come to the Day as a stranger to his servants. He knows their frame. He knows the cup of cold water no one saw and the tears nobody counted. Everything good in them he planted, watered and grew, and on that Day he will stand before the Father and praise his own work in them as though it were theirs. The Judge of all the earth will crown men and women with honour for gifts he gave them, and the whole universe will see that grace was never merely enough to save; it was enough to glorify.

verseByVerse.quote: I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?

I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers. Paul now explains what he has been doing all along. “Applied” is metaschēmatizō, to change the form of something, to transfer a figure. He has used himself and Apollos as the worked example, so that he would not have to name the leaders the Corinthians were actually quarrelling over. It is a pastor’s tact: he puts himself and his friend in the dock, two men who were plainly not rivals, so that the principle could be seen without anyone in Corinth being humiliated by name.

That you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written. The phrase is genuinely obscure, and honesty requires saying so. It may have been a known proverb, or a schoolroom expression about a child tracing letters and not straying outside the lines. What is clear is the direction. “What is written” is Scripture, which Paul has quoted again and again in chapters 1–3 (1:19, 31; 2:9, 16; 3:19–20). Scripture sets a boundary, and the Corinthians had wandered outside it. Their factions, their rankings, their confidence about who stands where, their worldly standards of wisdom and eloquence: all inventions, with no warrant in anything God has said. Whatever the idiom meant precisely, the instinct behind it is sound and permanent: stop at the line, and do not build convictions on ground Scripture has not given you.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Some churches hold that tradition or church authority has equal standing with Scripture, and so add doctrines Scripture does not teach. Verdict: Not going beyond what is written expresses the principle the Reformers called sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority for faith and life. Teachers and traditions are useful servants, but nothing may be required of Christians as necessary that is not taught in Scripture or drawn from it by good and necessary consequence (Westminster 1.6, 1.10).

That none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another. “Puffed up” is physioō, inflated like a pair of bellows, swollen with air. It is Paul’s favourite word for this church; he uses it six times in the letter (4:6, 18–19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4), and only once anywhere else. The image is exact: something enlarged by nothing, occupying more space than its substance justifies, and needing only a pinprick. And notice how the inflation worked. Nobody in Corinth was boasting in himself outright. They were boasting in their teacher: I am of Paul, I am of Apollos. It is the most respectable form of pride there is, to be proud of the man you follow, because it feels like loyalty. But it was really a claim that I, who chose the better teacher, am the better Christian.

For who sees anything different in you? Now verse 7, which is one of the great sentences of the New Testament, and which has done more to demolish spiritual pride than any argument ever constructed. Three questions, and there is no way through them. The first: what distinguishes you from the person you feel superior to? Who has made you differ? The question expects the answer: nobody, except God.

What do you have that you did not receive? The second question, and the honest answer is nothing whatever. Not your intelligence, which was in your genes before you could form a preference. Not your upbringing, or the country you were born in, or the family that told you about Christ, or the health that let you work, or the temperament that makes you easier to like. Not your knowledge, which came from teachers and books other people wrote. Not your faith, which Paul elsewhere says is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). Not your salvation, which was planned before the world began. Not one item on the list was generated by you. This is the doctrine of grace pressed down to the level of daily pride: the God who chose you, called you and kept you is the God who gave you every single thing you might be tempted to compare. Augustine said it was this very verse that finally convinced him that even the beginning of faith is God’s gift.

If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? The pride is not merely unattractive; it is a false claim. It presents a gift as an achievement, which is dishonesty as well as ingratitude. Boasting in a gift is absurd: you boast in the giver. And notice how completely this removes the ground for comparison, which is what the whole chapter has been about. You cannot rank yourself against another Christian on the basis of gifts you were both handed. It would be like two beggars quarrelling over which of them was the more distinguished for having been given a coat.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may never use books, confessions or creeds. These are helpful as long as they serve and agree with Scripture, and Paul himself handed on what he had received (15:3). Nor does verse 7 mean that gifts are imaginary or that we should pretend to have none. False modesty denies the gift and so dishonours the Giver just as surely as pride does.

Does this mean I should not feel good about hard work? No. Receiving everything does not make you passive. Paul worked harder than all the apostles, and in the same breath said it was not he but the grace of God that was with him (15:10). So you may be glad when you have worked hard and done well; gladness is not boasting. The difference is where the gladness goes. Pride stops at itself: look what I did. Gratitude travels on: look what God has given and done through me. When someone praises your work, you do not need to deny it or deflect it awkwardly. Thank them simply, and then, in your heart, hand the praise straight on to the One it belongs to.

In a sentence. Now, brothers and sisters, Paul has applied these things to himself and Apollos for your benefit, so that you may learn from us the meaning of the saying, “Do not go beyond what is written.” Then you will not be puffed up in being a follower of one of us over against the other. For who makes you different from anyone else? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?

On a Tuesday. This is the most useful single question in the letter for daily use. The next time you feel the small internal lift of being further on than another believer, better read, more disciplined, more sound, less of a mess, stop and ask Paul’s question in his words: what do I have that I did not receive? Follow it honestly for thirty seconds and the lift collapses, because every item you were about to congratulate yourself on turns out to have been handed to you. And what is left when it collapses is not humiliation but relief, and gratitude, and a strange new warmth towards the person you were just measuring (Romans 12:3; John 3:27).

For worship. Every good thing in every believer has a single address of origin. The faith that trusted, the eyes that were opened, the Bible on the shelf and the people who taught us to read it, the very breath with which we praise: all of it came down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change (James 1:17). And beneath every gift lies the Gift, the Son himself, given for us when we had nothing to offer but our need. He has left his people nothing to boast of except himself, and in him he has left them everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to irony. The Corinthians act as if they already have everything, already rich and reigning as kings without the apostles. He wishes they really did reign, so that the apostles could share it. Instead God seems to have put the apostles at the end of the procession, like men condemned to die in the arena, a spectacle to the world, to angels and to people. The apostles are fools for Christ, weak and dishonoured, while the Corinthians think themselves wise, strong and honoured. To this very hour the apostles are hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten and homeless; they work hard with their own hands; when cursed they bless, when persecuted they endure, when slandered they answer kindly. They have become like the world’s rubbish and the dirt everyone wipes off.
verseByVerse.theology:
Realized Eschatology and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Corinthians’ problem was not merely social pride but theological confusion about which age they were in. They were living as if the resurrection age had fully arrived — treating this present life as the time of reigning and riches. Paul’s corrective is eschatological: we are still in the “between the times,” the age between the first and second coming, in which the pattern of the Christian life is cruciform, not triumphant. The “not yet” of eschatology shapes the “how” of Christian living. Suffering, weakness, and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but participation in Christ’s own pattern — the pattern of resurrection that comes through, not around, the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman spectacle of condemned criminals paraded before the crowd before their execution is the image behind v. 9 (“a spectacle to the world”). Paul uses the imagery of the arena: God has made the apostles last, like the condemned criminals brought on at the end of the show. This was not hyperbole; Paul had been beaten, imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the contemporary version of Corinthian triumphalism: the claim that health, wealth, and success are the normal marks of Spirit-filled Christianity. Paul’s fools for Christ’s sake, hungry and homeless, are a permanent rebuke to any theology that makes suffering an anomaly rather than a participation in the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!

Already you have all you want! Three exclamations, and every one of them is irony. “All you want” is korennymi, to be full, satiated, to have eaten your fill. The Corinthians felt spiritually full: nothing lacking, nothing left to long for. And the repeated “already” is the key to the whole verse. It identifies their error with precision. They believed they had arrived.

Already you have become rich! Rich in gifts and knowledge (1:5), and proud of it. Paul himself had thanked God that they were enriched in every way, and they had taken the gift and turned it into a status. A congregation can be genuinely blessed and use the blessing as evidence that it no longer needs anything, least of all correction.

Without us you have become kings! They behaved as if they were already reigning, as believers will in the age to come (6:2–3; Revelation 5:10), and as if they had got there without needing the apostles. The riches, the reigning, the fullness, all the things Scripture promises for the age to come, they had claimed as present possessions. They were living as though the resurrection had happened, the kingdom had been consummated, and there was nothing left to wait for. This is sometimes called over-realised eschatology, which in plain words means claiming now the glory that belongs to the future. Paul does not deny that Christians are rich; he told them in the previous chapter that all things are theirs (3:21–22). What he denies is the timing. The inheritance is certain, and it has not yet been paid out. We are heirs in a country we have not yet entered, and to behave as though the crowns had already been handed out is not faith but confusion about which chapter of the story we are in.

Holy irony. Paul uses sarcasm here, deliberately and at length. Some readers are uncomfortable with that, but Scripture is not: Elijah on Carmel suggesting that Baal might be asleep or on a journey (1 Kings 18:27), Isaiah on idols that have to be carried by tired animals (Isaiah 46:1–7), the Lord himself on men who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Matthew 23:24). Irony is a legitimate instrument when someone is so pleased with himself that a straight statement will simply be absorbed. It holds a mirror at an angle the man cannot avoid. But it is a surgeon’s knife, not a toy, and Paul will explain in verse 14 why he used it: love.

And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you! Then the sentence turns and the irony breaks. The wistfulness is real. Paul is saying: I wish it were true. I wish the kingdom had come and the waiting were over, because I am hungry and cold and in trouble, and if you were really reigning then so would I be. His complaint is not that they are too hopeful. It is that they have taken delivery of a hope that has not yet arrived, and have therefore stopped needing the cross. It is not yet the time to reign. It is the time to suffer with Christ before being glorified with him (Romans 8:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have nothing now. In Christ we have every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3): forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, access to the Father, a foretaste of the age to come. The kingdom has truly arrived in Jesus. But the full glory is future, and the present is marked by the cross. Christians live between the already and the not yet, and the error at Corinth was to erase the second half.

So is it wrong to pray for healing or provision? No. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread, and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14). God often heals and often provides, and we should ask him boldly and thank him gladly. What this verse rules out is the teaching that health, wealth and victory are guaranteed now to anyone with enough faith, so that suffering becomes a sign that something has gone wrong with you. That is Corinthian triumphalism in modern dress. Paul’s answer to it is not a better argument. It is the next five verses, in which he lists what the apostles were actually enduring while the Corinthians reigned. Ask God for good things; do not tell him he owes them to you before the time.

In a sentence. Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! You have begun to reign, and that without us! How Paul wishes that you really had begun to reign, so that we also might reign with you!

On a Tuesday. Beware of a Christianity that promises everything now: health, wealth, triumph. The crown comes after the cross. Here is a test that goes deeper than doctrine. Ask what you have quietly come to expect from God in this life: not what you would say in a Bible study, but what you actually assume when things go wrong. If a serious disappointment feels like a breach of contract rather than a hard providence, then some part of you has been living in verse 8. The Christian has everything, and the payment date is not today (Romans 8:17–18; 2 Timothy 2:12).

For worship. There is a King who really does reign already, and he did not reach his throne by skipping the cross. He was hungry in the wilderness, homeless on the roads of Galilee, crowned with thorns before he was crowned with glory. Because he has gone ahead, the reign his people wait for is not a fantasy but a fixed date: if we endure, we will also reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12). The Lord who holds every crown has promised to share them, and he will not be one moment late.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks with irony: they acted as if the kingdom had already fully come.

verseByVerse.quote: For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men.

For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all. The imagery is from the arena, and it would have been unmistakable. “Exhibited” is apodeiknymi, to put on display. A day at the games ran in an order. The best contests came in the middle, when the crowd was fullest and most attentive. And at the end, when the spectacle proper was finished, the condemned were brought out: men with no weapons and no chance, whose function was not to compete but to die in front of people. Condemned prisoners were also paraded last in a Roman triumph, behind the spoils, on their way to execution. Paul says God has placed the apostles in that slot. Last of all.

Like men sentenced to death. “Sentenced to death” is epithanatios, condemned to die. The apostles lived under constant threat of death: Paul says elsewhere that he faced it every day (15:30–31) and was always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake (2 Corinthians 4:11). And set that against the previous verse. The Corinthians are reigning as kings; their founding apostle describes himself as the closing act of an execution. Those are not two styles of Christianity. One of them is a misunderstanding of what age we are in.

Because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men. The word for spectacle is theatron, theatre, show. Paul is not comparing himself to a gladiator, the professional with skill and a following, but to the man brought on at the end to be finished off. And then the audience, an arresting detail that is not decoration. Paul assumes that what happens to Christians is watched by the unseen order: the same assumption behind the angels who long to look into these things (1 Peter 1:12), and behind the claim that God intended his manifold wisdom to be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places through the church (Ephesians 3:10). Heaven is following this.

A lit stage. That puts a strange dignity on the least impressive Christian life. If the arena imagery is right, then the believer who is being quietly humiliated for his faith, passed over, laughed at, thought a fool, is not in an obscure corner of an indifferent universe. He is in the middle of a lit stage, being watched by beings who understand exactly what they are looking at, even when nobody in the room does. And it is worth asking what the angels are watching for. Not the suffering itself, which is common enough. What they cannot see anywhere except in the church is a creature who is losing and is not bitter: a man deprived of everything the world offers, who blesses the people taking it and does not stop trusting God. That has no natural explanation, and it is precisely what the next verses describe.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God despises his apostles or enjoys their suffering. He displays through their weakness the power of the cross: we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7–10; 12:9–10).

Are there apostles today? Not in the sense Paul means here. An apostle in this sense was a witness of the risen Christ, commissioned by him in person (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), and the apostles were part of the church’s foundation, which is laid once (Ephesians 2:20). The word is used more loosely in the New Testament of messengers sent out by churches (2 Corinthians 8:23; Philippians 2:25), and missionaries today stand in that line. But no one now can meet the qualifications of the Twelve and Paul, and no one should claim their authority. What the apostles taught is in Scripture, and that is how their office continues.

Are angels really watching me? Scripture says they are, though it does not tell us how much they see or understand. They rejoice over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10), they serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and they are learning the wisdom of God by watching the church (Ephesians 3:10). That is not meant to make you self-conscious, as if you were performing. It is meant to tell you that your faithfulness is not wasted. When you forgive someone who has not apologised, or keep trusting God in a hospital corridor, it is not happening in an empty room.

In a sentence. For it seems to Paul that God has put us apostles on display at the end of the procession, like those condemned to die in the arena. We have been made a spectacle to the whole universe, to angels as well as to human beings.

On a Tuesday. If you are suffering for Christ in some small, unseen way, the mocked faith at work, the unbelieving spouse, the slow cost of honesty, remember the audience. You are not forgotten in a corner. And ask the Lord, not to make your suffering impressive, but to make it a display of his grace: that what people see is not your strength but his.

For worship. Paul did not invent this pattern. There was One who was exhibited last of all, sentenced to death, made a spectacle before a jeering crowd, with the world and angels and men all watching. He was stripped and lifted up where everyone could see, and the whole city came out for the afternoon. And on that stage, before that audience, he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The condemned man at the end of the procession was the Conqueror leading it. His apostles are not in an unusual position for followers of that man. They are in the only position his followers have ever occupied, and it ends where his ended: on a throne.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned prisoners were paraded last in a Roman triumph, or sent into the arena at the end of the games.

verseByVerse.quote: We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.

We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. Three contrasts, laid out with painful symmetry. In each pair the apostles get the worse half, and in the last one Paul reverses the order so the sentence ends on disrepute. He is not distributing blame evenly. He is drawing a line between two ways of being Christian and putting himself firmly on the side nobody wants. “Fools for Christ’s sake” is the phrase to hold. Paul is not claiming that Christians are unintelligent, nor recommending eccentricity for its own sake. The foolishness is entirely derived: it is what you look like when you have staked everything on a crucified man, in a world that measures by power and success. The message is folly to those who are perishing (1:18); this is what it costs to be the man carrying it.

We are weak, but you are strong. The apostles are weak: Paul came to Corinth in weakness and fear and much trembling (2:3). The Corinthians think they are strong, and the irony is that this very sense of strength is their weakness.

You are held in honor, but we in disrepute. “Disrepute” is atimos, without honour, dishonoured. The Corinthians enjoyed status; the apostles were despised. And notice the asymmetry Paul is exposing. The Corinthians had managed to hold the gospel and their social standing at the same time. They were wise, strong, honoured: respectable in Corinth and confident in church. Paul’s implication is quiet and devastating: if the message is genuinely offensive, how have you avoided all the offence?

The question that has not aged. It is entirely possible to hold Christian convictions in a way that costs nothing: to believe the right things privately while making sure that nobody at work, in the family, or among one’s friends is ever given occasion to think one odd. It is not hypocrisy exactly. It is the careful management of the parts of the faith that would look foolish if said out loud. And this verse is also for the Christian who is already paying that cost, often in small and unglamorous ways. The colleague known as the religious one, whose views are treated as a harmless quirk. The student whose position on some question has quietly ended his hope of being taken seriously. The relative whose family have decided, kindly, that he has become a bit much. None of that is persecution in the sense the early church knew, and it should not be dressed up as martyrdom. But it is real, and it wears people down precisely because it is so ordinary. Paul’s word to such a reader is that being thought a fool for Christ’s sake is not a sign that you have handled things badly. It is a sign you are in the apostolic line.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians really were wise and strong. Paul is exposing their pride: they had taken on the world’s values and called them spiritual. Nor does it mean the Christian should seek to be disliked. Being despised for Christ is an honour; being despised for rudeness is not.

How do I know whether I am a fool for Christ or just foolish? Ask what the offence is attached to. If people think you odd because you will not lie for the company, because you go to church, because you believe Jesus rose and is the only way to the Father, that is the foolishness of the cross. If they think you odd because you are harsh, preachy, careless about your work or quick to take offence, that is your own foolishness, and it is a burden to the gospel, not a badge (1 Peter 4:15–16). Paul was courteous, hard-working and wise in how he spoke (Colossians 4:5–6). The goal is that if they reject you, they should be rejecting Christ in you, not the rough edges round him.

In a sentence. We are fools for Christ, but you are so wise in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are honoured, we are dishonoured!

On a Tuesday. If following Christ costs you reputation, you are walking where the apostles walked. So here is a test that is easier to state than to pass. Name the belief you hold that would make you look most foolish among the people whose respect you most want. Then ask when you last said it out loud in front of them. The answer is not a verdict: there is wisdom in when and how to speak, and Paul was no boor. But if the answer is never, and the reason is not love but reputation, then the honour in this verse is in the wrong column (1:18–25; Hebrews 13:13).

For worship. Christ crucified is the wisdom of God and the power of God, and the world looked at him and saw a fool on a cross. He was despised and rejected, a man from whom men hid their faces, and he endured the shame for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Every Christian who is laughed at for his name shares a little of the disgrace that he bore in full. And the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men (1:25): the day is coming when the fools for Christ will be seen to have been the only wise people in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.

To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless. Now the catalogue, and it is deliberately physical. Paul is not recalling his early hardships from a comfortable retirement. To the present hour: this is his condition as he writes. Hunger, thirst, ragged clothes, beatings, and no settled home. “Buffeted” is kolaphizō, struck with the fist, the very word used when the soldiers struck Jesus in the high priest’s house (Matthew 26:67). The apostle carries in his body the bruises his Lord received first.

And we labor, working with our own hands. This carries a sting a modern reader misses. In the Greek world manual work was contemptible; a philosopher who worked with his hands had lowered himself, and the professional speakers who toured Corinth were paid handsomely for talking. Paul made tents (Acts 18:3; 20:34). Part of the Corinthian embarrassment about their apostle was straightforwardly social: their founder had a trade and calloused hands. He accepted it so as not to put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (9:12).

When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. Here is the heart of the passage. Look at what is not there: no retaliation, no defence of reputation, no cutting reply, no campaign to set the record straight. And notice that these responses are not passive. To bless is actively to ask God’s good for the man who has just insulted you. To endure is to stay put under the pressure rather than escape it. To entreat (parakaleō) is to speak kindly, to appeal, to keep the door open towards someone spreading lies about you. That is harder than a counter-attack and takes longer. It is exactly what Paul had been taught: bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you (Luke 6:28). And it is what he had seen in his Lord, who when he was reviled did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23), and who from the cross asked the Father to forgive the men who had nailed him there (Luke 23:34).

We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things. Then the final image, and Paul chooses the two ugliest words available. Perikatharma is what is wiped off when something is cleaned, the filth in the bucket. Peripsēma is scrapings, the residue on the cloth. Both words were also used of the lowest of criminals, sometimes thrown out or sacrificed to purge a city in time of disaster, the human rubbish the city could afford to lose. The apostles are treated as human garbage. And this is how Paul lists his credentials. Not the visions, not the miracles, not the churches planted, though he had all three. When Paul wants to prove he is a genuine apostle to a church impressed by success, he produces his hunger and his ruined reputation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be homeless or poor, or that suffering is to be sought for its own sake. It means that faithfulness to Christ can cost everything, and apostolic ministry did. Where the cost comes, it is not a sign of God’s absence but of fellowship with the crucified Lord.

Does blessing those who revile me mean I must let people abuse me? No. Paul is describing how to answer insult, slander and persecution for the gospel’s sake: with blessing instead of revenge. He is not telling anyone to remain under abuse at home, at work or in a church. Paul himself appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen when he was being illegally beaten (Acts 22:25), and when his life was threatened he escaped (Acts 9:25). Abuse should never be tolerated, and the right response to it includes getting to safety, telling those who can protect you, and reporting crimes to the authorities, who are God’s servants for that very purpose (Romans 13:4). You can pray for God’s good for an abuser, and refuse to retaliate, from a place of safety. Blessing is not the same as staying.

Should pastors then work for a living instead of being paid? Not necessarily. Paul says plainly that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (9:14), and he accepted gifts from other churches (Philippians 4:15–16). He chose to work in Corinth so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money in a city full of paid speakers (9:12, 15–18). Some ministers today rightly work a trade, and others are rightly supported by their churches. The principle is not the payslip but the heart: a minister must never preach for gain, and a church must never let its minister go in need.

In a sentence. To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are in rags, we are brutally treated, we are homeless. We work hard with our own hands. When we are cursed, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure it; when we are slandered, we answer kindly. We have become the scum of the earth, the garbage of the world, right up to this moment.

On a Tuesday. These three responses are learnable and can be practised this week. Somebody will misrepresent you. Somebody will say something dismissive. The instinct will be to answer, and the answer will be drafted in your head within about four seconds. Paul’s three verbs are the alternative, and they are specific enough to act on: ask God to do that person good, by name; stay where God has put you rather than withdrawing in a sulk; keep speaking to them rather than about them (Romans 12:14, 20–21; 1 Peter 3:9). And give thanks for those who suffered to bring you the gospel, and pray this week for Christians who are being treated as the refuse of the world in places where faith can still cost a life.

For worship. None of this is natural, and that is the point. A man can be reduced to the scrapings of the world and still be blessing the people who put him there, and only one thing in the universe produces that. It is not strength of character. It is the life of the crucified Christ in his servants. He was the One truly treated as the refuse of all things, taken outside the city and put to death so that the city might be cleansed, and he did not revile. He was struck with the fist and answered with a prayer for his enemies. The blessing that comes from Paul’s lips in the dust of Corinth flows from the blessing that came from the cross, and it is the blessing in which every believer now stands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he is not writing to shame them but to warn them as his dear children. They may have countless guardians in Christ, but they do not have many fathers; through the gospel Paul became their father in Christ Jesus. So he urges them to imitate him. That is why he is sending Timothy, his loved and faithful son in the Lord, to remind them of his way of life in Christ, which he teaches in every church. Some have become arrogant, as though Paul were not coming. But he will come soon, if the Lord wills, and find out not what these proud people say but what power they have, because God’s kingdom is not a matter of talk but of power. Which do they want: that he come with a rod, or with love and a gentle spirit?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fatherhood of the Apostle and Spiritual Formation by Imitation

Paul’s claim to spiritual fatherhood over the Corinthian church is grounded in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The new birth produces a spiritual parentage — and the one through whose proclamation the Spirit brought new birth to a community is, in a real sense, their spiritual father. This is not about control but about formation. Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living embodiment of the gospel he preached — not his person but his pattern, the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had, in Paul’s absence, developed arrogant teachers who had dismissed the apostle. Timothy is sent to embody what Paul had taught by his life — because argument alone, without the living example, is insufficient. Now: The pastoral call to “be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1) is the most demanding thing a minister can say — and the most necessary. Disciples need models, not merely doctrines. The church that produces only correct theology without cruciform character has missed the point of the apostolic office.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel.

I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. The irony stops, and the change of tone is one of the most affecting moments in the letter. Everything since verse 8, the sarcasm about kings, the arena, the scrapings of the world, has to be re-read in the light of this sentence. It was not the retaliation of a man whose pride had been injured. It was a father who could not get through to his children, doing the one thing left. And the distinction he draws is worth pausing on, because we habitually confuse the two. Shaming and admonishing feel similar from the outside and are opposite in intent. Shame attacks the person: it aims to make him feel small, and it produces either compliance or resentment and never growth. Admonition (noutheteō, to put in mind, to warn and counsel) attacks the problem. It aims at change, and it can only be received from someone the hearer is sure loves him.

For though you have countless guides in Christ. “Countless” is literally ten thousand. The word for guides is paidagōgoi: the household slave who walked the children to school, kept them out of trouble and enforced the rules (Galatians 3:24). Useful, necessary, and hired. Not a parent. Many teachers had come and gone in Corinth, and Paul is not sneering at them. He is naming a different kind of bond.

You do not have many fathers. Tutors can be hired; a father is unique. Paul’s relationship to them is deeper than any later teacher’s, because of how it began.

For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel. “Became your father” is egennēsa, from gennaō, I begot you. Through Paul’s preaching of the gospel God gave them new birth, and Paul was the instrument of it. The man through whose preaching you were born cannot be replaced by a better speaker, any more than a father can be replaced by a more impressive man. That is worth saying to a church culture in which people move between congregations for the quality of the teaching, and to anyone who has quietly transferred their loyalty from the person who led them to Christ to somebody more polished. The polished man may well teach you more. He will never be the one who told you first.

Where Christians differ: calling ministers father. Jesus said to call no one on earth your father (Matthew 23:9), yet Paul calls himself their father. Some use this to justify the title Father for priests. Verdict: Jesus forbade giving any human the place of ultimate spiritual authority that belongs only to God. Paul is describing a relationship, not claiming a title or rank. He brought them to new birth through the gospel, and cares for them with a father’s love (1 Thessalonians 2:11; Philemon 10). The word describes affection and responsibility, not a priestly office, and he uses it to plead, not to rule. The verse gives no warrant for making Father an honorific for ministers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul has authority over their faith in place of Christ: not that we lord it over your faith, he says, but we work with you for your joy (2 Corinthians 1:24). He is a father in Christ, through the gospel, and the life he passed on was never his own.

How to correct someone. There is a practical lesson here about how to correct anyone at all. Notice the order Paul uses. He speaks the hard thing first, at length, without softening it, and then makes the affection explicit. He does not open with reassurance to cushion the blow, and he does not leave the affection to be inferred. He says it: beloved children. Most of us get this wrong in one of two directions. Either the love is assumed and never stated, so the rebuke arrives as bare criticism and lands as shame. Or the love is stated so warmly and at such length that the correction never actually gets said, and everybody leaves comfortable and nothing changes.

What if the person who led me to Christ later fell away or hurt me? Then grieve, but do not doubt what God did. The new birth is God’s work, not the messenger’s; Paul was only the instrument, and God can use a cracked vessel to carry living water (Philippians 1:15–18). Your faith does not depend on the one who brought it to you, but on the Christ he pointed to. If that person sinned against you, you are not bound to stay close or to pretend nothing happened, and if they did harm, it should be dealt with honestly. But you may still thank God for the gospel you heard through them, and pray that he would restore them.

In a sentence. Paul is writing this not to shame you but to warn you as his dear children. Even if you had ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers, for in Christ Jesus he became your father through the gospel.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have helped bring to faith or grow in Christ? Care for them like a parent: with warmth, patience and honest warning. And if there is something you need to say to someone, ask whether they know, not whether they could reasonably infer, but whether they know because you have told them, that you are for them. If they do not, the correction will not land however true it is. If they do, you can say almost anything. Paul had just called them puffed-up infants playing at kings, and he could do it because they had watched him work with his hands among them and knew exactly what he had spent on them (Proverbs 27:6; 2 Corinthians 12:14–15).

For worship. Behind the father in Christ stands the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope (1 Peter 1:3). Every spiritual father is only a midwife at a birth God brings about. And the warnings of a father in God are themselves a mercy, for the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). Many guides may come and go, but the Father who begot us by the word of truth never changes, and he has never once spoken to his children except in love.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guides” was used of the household slave who took charge of children on their way to school.

verseByVerse.quote: I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I urge you, then, be imitators of me. That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church.

I urge you, then, be imitators of me. On a first reading it sounds breathtakingly presumptuous. No modern minister would dare say it, and our instinct is to reach for a qualification. Paul does supply one, later in the letter: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (11:1). So the imitation is not of a personality but of a direction; he is a man pointing, and he is asking them to follow the pointing. “Imitators” is mimētai, from which we get mimic. Children learn by copying their father, and Paul has just called himself their father. But notice that he does not soften it here, and that our discomfort with the sentence may say more about us than about him.

What he is asking them to copy. Consider what he is asking them to imitate. He has just spent six verses describing it, and it is not his eloquence, his authority or his success. It is hunger, disrepute, manual labour, and blessing people who revile you. Imitate me, in this context, means: take the lower place, work with your hands, be thought a fool, and do not retaliate. That is not a bid for a following. Nobody builds a personality cult on that material. And there is a reason the appeal has to be to a life rather than a syllabus. Most of these people had no Scriptures of their own, and many could not read. Christianity had to be passed on the way a trade is passed on, by watching somebody do it. That is still how most of it is actually learned. Nobody has ever become patient by reading about patience; they have watched a patient person handle something and understood, for the first time, that it was possible.

That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. Timothy, Paul’s spiritual son (1 Timothy 1:2), was on his way to Corinth (16:10). Paul does not send a letter alone. He sends a person, and the person he sends is himself a demonstration, a man formed by exactly the pattern under dispute. The argument travels in a document; the pattern travels in a man.

To remind you of my ways in Christ. “Ways” (hodoi, paths) means Paul’s manner of life and teaching, his patterns as a Christian. Timothy is not bringing new doctrine. He is bringing a reminder, a living copy of what they had already seen.

As I teach them everywhere in every church. Paul did not have special teaching for Corinth. He taught the same things in all the churches (7:17; 11:16; 14:33). It is a quiet answer to the suggestion that Corinth was being given a harder standard than everyone else, and to the pride that thought Corinth could be an exception. There is one gospel and one pattern of life, the same in Ephesus and Philippi and here.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was arrogant or sinless. He called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). He calls them to imitate his imitation of Christ, and wherever he fails to look like Christ, Christ is the pattern, not Paul.

Is it arrogant for me to say “follow my example”? Not if it is said in Paul’s spirit and about Paul’s pattern. Every parent, elder and older believer is already being imitated whether they like it or not; the only question is whether they will own it. Elders are told to be examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and older women to train younger women by their lives (Titus 2:3–5). You do not need to claim perfection. You can say: watch how I bring my failures to Christ, how I handle money, how I speak about people who are absent. That is not boasting. It is the honest admission that Christianity is caught as well as taught.

What if there is no one in my church I can imitate? There almost certainly is, but they may not be where you are looking. The people worth imitating are rarely the most visible. Look for the faithful rather than the impressive: the couple who have quietly loved each other for forty years, the widow who prays, the man who never speaks badly of anyone. Ask to spend time with them. Read the lives of faithful Christians from the past, too (Hebrews 13:7). And remember that the final pattern is Christ himself, whom every human example only points to.

In a sentence. Therefore Paul urges you to imitate him. For this reason he has sent to you Timothy, his son whom he loves, who is faithful in the Lord. He will remind you of his way of life in Christ Jesus, which agrees with what he teaches everywhere in every church.

On a Tuesday. Two tests, and both are uncomfortable in the right way. First: who are you actually imitating? Not who do you admire in the abstract, but whose life have you got close enough to see, and whose handling of money, marriage, disappointment and provocation is shaping yours? Most Christians are being formed by somebody, and a great many are being formed at a distance by people they have only ever seen performing. Second, harder: is there anyone who could learn Christianity by watching you? Not by asking your opinions; by watching. That is the question Paul’s sentence puts to every parent, every elder and every long-standing member of a congregation, and it cannot be answered by improving one’s doctrine alone (Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:6).

For worship. Paul was not afraid to be copied, because what he offered to be copied was a cross, and the cross was not his. Behind every faithful life stands the one Life that can be imitated without reserve: the Son who did nothing on his own but only what he saw the Father doing (John 5:19), who left us an example so that we might follow in his steps (1 Peter 2:21). Every saint worth copying is a copy of him. He is the original, and by his Spirit he is still making copies, one disciple at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.

Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. The diagnosis is shrewd, and it names something universal: people behave differently when they believe they will not be met. The word is the puffed-up word again, physioō, inflated. And the inflation had a cause: distance. Paul was across the Aegean in Ephesus. Some had been saying he would not dare return; he sends letters and Timothy, but stays away. So they felt free to ignore him, and a certain confidence had grown up in Corinth, of the sort that always grows in the absence of the person who might answer back. It is the courage of the letter never delivered to the man’s face.

But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. Paul’s reply is simply to announce that the absence is temporary, and the whole basis of their confidence disappears with the sentence. He does intend to come (16:5). But notice the words he attaches: if the Lord wills. This is not a verbal tic. It is the settled habit of a man who does not consider his own plans self-executing, the same instinct James insists on: you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:15). Paul is in the middle of asserting his authority over a rebellious church, and even here he will not say he is coming without adding that it is not finally up to him. A man who says that about a journey has already settled something about who runs the world, and it shows up in his diary rather than only in his theology.

And I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power. Two words are set against each other: logos and dynamis, talk and power. Talk is impressive speech, the very thing Corinth prized. Power is the real working of God’s Spirit in a life. Paul is not coming to compare rhetoric; the Corinthians would win that, and it would prove nothing. He is coming to see whether anything has actually changed: whether the gospel these people discuss so fluently has produced in them what it always produces where it is real. What that is, the letter has already told us and will tell us again. Chapter 3 said that jealousy and strife were the evidence of the flesh (3:3); chapter 13 will say that gifts without love are nothing. So the power Paul means to look for is not first the spectacular. It is whether these people have begun to love each other.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words are unimportant. Paul’s ministry was a ministry of the word, and the gospel is a message that must be spoken. But words without the Spirit’s power are empty, and the Spirit’s power always comes through the word, not around it (1 Thessalonians 1:5).

Must I always say “if the Lord wills”? It is not a formula you must attach to every sentence; Paul often speaks of his plans without it (16:8). It is an attitude of the heart that should be visible in how you plan. Make plans, work hard at them, and hold them with an open hand, knowing that you do not know what tomorrow will bring (James 4:13–16). Saying the words aloud now and then is a good discipline, because it reminds you and others who is in charge. What matters is that you would not be shocked, or bitter, if God redrew the map.

In a sentence. Some of you have become arrogant, as if Paul were not coming to you. But he will come to you very soon, if the Lord is willing, and then he will find out not only what these arrogant people are saying, but what power they have.

On a Tuesday. Does your life have real spiritual power behind your words: love, patience, holiness? A man can talk about grace for thirty years with real fluency and be no easier to live with than he was at the start. Talk is cheap and endlessly available; the other thing cannot be produced on demand. So ask those who live with you, not those who hear you teach, whether they see it. And there is a second test, which needs no theology at all: listen to how you talk about next year. Ask God for the power, and for the humility to say, if the Lord wills.

For worship. The Lord who will come to his church does not need to find out anything: he walks among the lampstands with eyes like a flame of fire (Revelation 2:18), and he is coming soon. His word is never empty talk. He spoke, and the world was made; he speaks, and the dead hear his voice and live (John 5:25). The power Paul looked for in Corinth is his power, the same power that raised Christ from the dead, now at work in jars of clay, and it is never once found without love.

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?

For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. It is the principle behind the visit, stated as a maxim. The kingdom of God is God’s rule, present now through Christ and the Spirit, and it shows itself not in eloquent religious talk but in changed lives (Romans 14:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). And it cuts in both directions. Against the Corinthians: fluency is not evidence of anything. They could discuss wisdom, argue about apostles and produce impressive religious conversation, and Paul says the kingdom is not made of that material. Words are the cheapest thing in any church, and the ability to talk well about God has never yet transformed anybody who possessed it.

Not a demand for the spectacular. But it cuts against another error too. “Power” here is not a promise of the spectacular, and it should not be conscripted to demand signs and wonders as the proof of a genuine church. The power this letter has described is the power of God that saves through a message about an execution (1:18), that will raise the dead (6:14), and that turns a jealous congregation into people who love each other. That is not less than miraculous; it is simply harder to photograph.

What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod? Then the final question, and Paul leaves it hanging as a question rather than a threat. The rod is a father’s rod of discipline (Proverbs 13:24). The rod is real: Paul has apostolic authority and will use it, as chapter 5 is about to show. Nothing in this chapter’s tenderness cancels the discipline. A father who can never be firm is not being kind, and a church that can never act is not being loving.

Or with love in a spirit of gentleness? Gentleness is prautēs: meekness, mildness, strength under control. Notice that both the rod and gentleness are love; but gentleness is what Paul longs to use. And notice that the choice is not his. He has put it in their hands: what do you wish? This is the strangest kind of authority, a man with the right to compel, asking. He would rather arrive as a father with nothing in his hand, and whether he can depends entirely on what they do between receiving this letter and seeing him. That is exactly how God deals with his people throughout Scripture. He warns before he acts, at length, and the warning is itself the mercy: a rod described in advance is a rod trying not to be used. Turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die (Ezekiel 33:11)?

What it does not mean. It does not mean that discipline is unloving. Loving fathers discipline (Hebrews 12:6). But they prefer to see children respond to gentleness, and they never discipline in anger for their own satisfaction.

Does God still come to his children with the rod? Yes, but always as a Father, never as an executioner. The Lord disciplines those he loves, and the discipline of believers is not punishment for sin, which Christ has already borne, but training for holiness (Hebrews 12:5–11). It can come through hardship, through the loss of comfort, through the exposure of sin, or through the discipline of the church. It is painful, and it is always for our good, that we may share his holiness. The quickest way to be spared the rod is to respond to the word: when God speaks gently, listen.

Is church discipline really loving? It is, when it is done in the right way, and the next chapter shows why. Discipline is meant to bring a sinner to repentance, to protect the church, and to honour Christ’s name (5:5–7). It must be carried out by the church in a patient, ordered way (Matthew 18:15–17), with humility and with the aim of restoring, not removing. A church that never disciplines is not kinder than one that does; it is simply leaving people to wander towards danger without a warning.
