Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary:
So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?

So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? “Those who have no standing” translates exouthenēmenoi: the despised, those counted as nothing in the church. In the ESV reading they are the pagan judges, whose values the church does not share and to whom it does not look for wisdom. Why, then, would Christians hand them their family quarrels?

Question or command? Verse 4 can be read two ways. The ESV takes it as a question: why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church, that is, before pagan judges? Older translations read it as an ironic command: appoint even the least regarded members of the church to judge. The ESV reading is the more likely, because Paul goes straight on to ask whether there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute (v. 5). Either way the point is the same: the church should be able to settle these matters itself.

I say this to your shame. Paul does not reach for that phrase often, and when he does the rebuke has reached its sharpest point. He used the opposite formula two chapters ago: I do not write these things to make you ashamed (4:14). Here he does. The Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom, and Paul says they should be ashamed.

Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers? The irony would have been unbearable, and it is the whole point. This is the church that has spent four chapters congratulating itself on its wisdom (1:5; 3:18). They had factions organised around competing teachers; they prided themselves on knowledge and eloquence; they thought of themselves as the mature. Now Paul simply asks them to produce one wise man for a practical purpose, and the answer, evidently, is that they cannot. It is the standing test of whether wisdom is real. Wisdom that can discuss the deep things of God and cannot help two brothers settle a debt is not wisdom in any sense the Bible recognises. James makes the same point from the other end: the wisdom from above is peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy, and where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, whatever else is present, it is not wisdom (James 3:14–17).

But brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers? The last phrase carries the second injury. Double shame: brothers fighting, and doing it in public, in front of exactly the people the church exists to reach. Think of what a Corinthian pagan would have seen. A new movement claiming that its God had reconciled enemies and made one body out of Jew and Greek, slave and free, and two of its members in the basilica, arguing about money, using the same lawyers and the same tactics as everybody else. Every claim the church had made about itself was being tested in that courtroom, and it was failing.

The modern courtroom. This has more forms now than Paul could have imagined. Congregations split in public. Churches conduct their disagreements where anyone can read them. Christians savage one another in writing, at length, before an audience of thousands, over matters that two people of goodwill in one room could have resolved in an afternoon. The watching world does not weigh the arguments. It notices that these people cannot get on, and it concludes that their message of reconciliation does not work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders have the power of a civil court. The church can mediate and advise, and discipline members who refuse to be reconciled. It cannot fine, imprison or enforce, and it must never try to handle crimes itself.

What does settling a dispute inside the church look like in practice? Notice what Paul assumes the church should have: a working way of settling disputes between its members. Not a court, but wise people the parties are willing to be bound by. In practice, the two people first talk privately (Matthew 18:15). If that fails, they agree together to bring in one or two mature, impartial believers, often elders or people they both trust, and they agree in advance to accept their counsel. Some Christians use trained Christian mediators or arbitrators, whose agreements can also be recognised in law. The aim is not merely a ruling but reconciliation, with honesty about wrongs done on both sides.

In a sentence. Therefore, if you have disputes about such matters, do you ask for a ruling from those whose way of life is scorned in the church? Paul says this to shame you. Is it possible that there is nobody among you wise enough to judge a dispute between believers? But instead, one brother takes another to court, and this in front of unbelievers!

On a Tuesday. Churches should have wise people ready to help members settle disputes. Pray that yours does, and be one of them. And here is a practical question for any church, answerable in a sentence. If two members of your congregation had a genuine, sharp, money-shaped disagreement next month, who would they take it to, and would they accept the answer? If the honest reply is that there is no such person and no such process, then this passage is not describing Corinth’s problem. It is describing yours (James 3:13–18; Matthew 18:15–17).

For worship. The wisdom the Corinthians could not find among themselves is found in full in Christ, who became to us wisdom from God (1:30). He is the great peacemaker, who made peace by the blood of his cross and reconciled enemies to God and to one another (Colossians 1:20; Ephesians 2:14–16). Where his people let him rule their quarrels, the world sees what it has never seen elsewhere: brothers who were wronged and forgave, and enemies who sit at one table. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God, because they look like the Son.

parallels.desc: able men to judge the people

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary:
To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud—even your own brothers!

To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. The word is hēttēma: a loss, a defeat, a failure. Paul is saying that the verdict is irrelevant, because the outcome was settled the moment the case was filed. Win or lose, you have lost. Whoever wins the case, the church has already lost. The very existence of such lawsuits shows a failure of love.

Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? Then two questions that are among the most countercultural sentences in the New Testament. Paul is not asking them to pretend the wrong did not happen. The words are blunt: be wronged, be cheated. They assume a real injury and a real loss. What he is proposing is that a Christian might decide to absorb it. The logic is not passivity but a different arithmetic. The Corinthian litigant has calculated that the disputed sum is worth more than the brother. Paul says the calculation is wrong, and that a man shaped by the cross will reach a different total, because the one he follows absorbed infinite wrong without retaliating, and when he was reviled did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). It is the Sermon on the Mount applied to a courtroom: if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well (Matthew 5:39–40). Better to lose money than to lose a brother and dishonour Christ. It is a radical, cross-shaped answer.

But you yourselves wrong and defraud, even your own brothers! Then the sharpest sentence in the paragraph. Paul has been addressing the plaintiffs. Now he turns to the defendants, and the picture is complete. This is not a church of innocent parties being unfairly pursued. Some of them were not the victims but the cheaters. They were defrauding fellow believers, and doing it to their own brothers, perhaps using the courts to do it, and were then apparently surprised to find themselves in court.

Where Christians differ: may a Christian ever sue a Christian? Some say never, under any circumstances. Others say the courts are open to Christians like anyone else. Verdict: Paul’s rule is that disputes between believers should be settled within the church, and that it is often better to accept loss than to sue a brother. But this assumes both parties are willing to submit to the church. Where a professing believer refuses church correction, he is to be treated as an unbeliever (Matthew 18:17), and there may be cases where legal protection is necessary, especially for the vulnerable, or where crimes are involved. Abuse, violence and fraud should be reported to the authorities whom God appointed to punish evil (Romans 13:4).

A guard against misuse. A guard is essential here, because this passage has been used to do real harm, and the misuse is not hypothetical. These verses are about property and money disputes between Christian brothers. They are not a rule that Christians must never use the law, and they cannot be stretched into one without contradicting Scripture and Paul himself. Paul invoked his Roman citizenship when he was about to be flogged (Acts 22:25), demanded a public apology from the magistrates at Philippi (Acts 16:37), and appealed to Caesar rather than be handed over (Acts 25:11). In Romans he says the civil authority is God’s servant, who bears the sword to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), which is not something God instituted so that his people should never use it. So this text has nothing to say against reporting a crime, nothing against protecting a child, nothing against a victim of abuse or assault going to the police, or an employee taking a genuine grievance to a tribunal. Any leader who quotes “why not rather suffer wrong?” to persuade a victim to stay silent and keep it in the church has taken a verse about a money dispute and used it as a lid. That is the opposite of what the passage intends, since the whole point is that the strong should stop using their advantage against the weak.

What it does not mean. It does not mean victims of crime should stay silent to protect the church’s reputation. That would be a grave misuse of this passage.

Does suffering wrong mean I must let someone go on cheating me? No. Choosing to absorb a loss, rather than sue a brother, is not the same as enabling ongoing wrong. You may forgive a debt and still decline to lend again. You may let go of a grievance and still end a business partnership with someone who has been dishonest. You may, and sometimes must, warn others or bring the matter to the church, so that the person is called to repent and others are protected (Matthew 18:15–17). Love does not pretend that wrong is right. It simply refuses revenge, and it cares more about the brother’s soul and Christ’s honour than about winning.

In a sentence. The very fact that you have lawsuits among you means you have been completely defeated already. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated? Instead, you yourselves cheat and do wrong, and you do this to your brothers and sisters.

On a Tuesday. The test cuts both ways, and it is worth running honestly. If you are the one who has been wronged, could you absorb it, genuinely, without keeping a running account? And if you are honest, is there anyone with a legitimate grievance against you: money owed, a promise not kept, an advantage taken because you could? Put it right this week. The chapter began by asking who would judge the case. It ends by suggesting that both men in the courtroom may need the same verdict (Matthew 5:38–42; Romans 12:17–19).

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the one man who never wronged anyone and was wronged by everyone. He was defrauded of his clothes at the foot of a cross, and he did not sue. He was tried by an unrighteous court, and he did not appeal. He suffered wrong, not because he could not defend himself, but because he was buying back the very people who had wronged him. We were the ones who defrauded God of the honour we owed him, and he did not take us to court. He took our place in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to be deceived: the unrighteous will not inherit God’s kingdom. Those who live in sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery or homosexual practice, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, slanderers and swindlers will not inherit it. Some of the Corinthians had lived exactly like that. But they were washed, set apart as holy and declared righteous in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The triad of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — covers the full scope of soteric transformation. Reformed theology typically orders justification before sanctification logically; Paul here places sanctification before justification in the list, which suggests he is not giving a logical order but a rhetorical one: moving from the most experientially tangible (washing, cleansing from the pollution of past sin) to the most legally decisive (justification, right standing before God). All three are accomplished “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — trinitarian to the root.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street — not foreign or distant behaviour but the lives many of the congregation had lived and from which the gospel had extracted them. Paul is not writing to people who need to be warned away from exotic sins; he is reminding them of who they used to be, so they understand what they now are. Now: The church in every generation contains people whose past is on the list in vv. 9–10. The three words of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — are the most liberating words any of them will ever hear about that past. It was real; the transformation is realer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? There is a link with verses 1–8 that English hides. The “unrighteous” (adikoi) are the same word as the pagan judges of verse 1, and those who wrong their brothers in verse 8 are doing adikeō, acting unrighteously. Paul is saying: you are behaving like the very people you took your case to, and you know where they are heading. To inherit the kingdom is to receive eternal life in God’s coming reign, to have a share in the age to come. And “will not inherit” is the whole weight of the sentence. Not will be less rewarded. The vocabulary is of inheritance: of having no share at all.

Do not be deceived. The warning implies that someone was doing the deceiving. Given what this letter has shown of Corinth, the likely message was that grace is so complete and freedom so total that conduct has become a secondary matter; that how you lived did not matter if you had knowledge or gifts. Paul says that is a lie, and that people were believing it. It is still being told, in many forms, and it is still a lie.

Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers. The sexually immoral (pornoi) are those who commit any sexual sin outside marriage. Idolaters are worshippers of other gods. Adulterers (moichoi) are those unfaithful to their marriage. Before going further, read the list as a whole, because how it is read decides whether it is heard rightly.

Nor men who practice homosexuality. The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind this phrase refer to the passive and active partners in consensual homosexual acts. Readers deserve to know what is actually there. Malakoi means literally soft ones, and in Greco-Roman usage it commonly denoted the passive partner in male same-sex intercourse; older versions rendered it effeminate, which is misleading to a modern ear. Arsenokoitai is a compound of arsēn (male) and koitē (bed), literally male-bedders, and appears to have been coined from the Greek Old Testament of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where those two words stand side by side in the prohibition of a man lying with a male. Together they cover both roles in the act, and Paul uses the terms to cover homosexual acts generally.

Nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers. Sins of property and speech too: theft, greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse, extortion. The list is broad. Nine items, and only three of them are sexual. Sitting alongside them are greed, drunkenness, verbal abuse and dishonest dealing: sins that are present in every congregation that has ever existed and are almost never preached with this level of seriousness. Paul has assembled a list on which nearly everybody appears somewhere. No one can look down on others. A church that reads it as a description of outsiders, or of one particular group, has misread it so completely that the next verse will make no sense at all.

Will inherit the kingdom of God. Those whose lives are characterised by these sins, unrepentant, show they are not God’s people. And here the grammar matters enormously, because it is where most of the pastoral damage is done. Every item in this list is a settled way of life, not an experience of temptation. Paul is describing what people are and do, habitually and without repentance: the thief who steals, the drunkard who drinks, the reviler whose tongue is his weapon.

Where Christians differ: homosexuality. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative relationships, such as pederasty or prostitution, not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Verdict: The terms Paul uses draw directly on Leviticus, which forbids homosexual acts as such, without reference to exploitation. Paul also names both partners rather than only the exploiter, which an argument about exploitation would not require. Elsewhere Paul grounds his teaching in creation (Romans 1:26–27), and Jesus defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman (Matthew 19:4–6). The historic Christian teaching is that sexual relations belong only within marriage between a man and a woman. This must be held with deep compassion. Same-sex attraction is a real and often painful experience, not chosen, and believers who experience it and live faithfully are brothers and sisters to be loved and supported. Homosexual sin is listed alongside greed, drunkenness and slander, sins all of us need forgiveness for. And verse 11 shows the gospel’s welcome to all.

Temptation is not practice. If you are a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction and is not acting on it, who has perhaps fought this for years, told almost nobody, and reads this verse with dread every time it is preached, understand that you are not the person described here. Temptation is not practice. A desire resisted is not a life lived. The man in this list is not fighting; he has settled. And a believer who is fighting is doing exactly what the next verse says the gospel produces. The same distinction applies right along the list, and applies to everyone. Being tempted to greed is not greed. Losing your temper is not being a reviler. What Paul is warning against is not the presence of a struggle but the absence of one: the comfortable conviction that a person may practise what he likes and inherit the kingdom anyway. That is the deception, and it is why he opened with do not be deceived (Galatians 5:19–21; Ephesians 5:5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that anyone who has ever done one of these things is lost. Verse 11 says some of them were such people. It means that unrepentant, habitual practice of such sins is incompatible with belonging to God’s kingdom.

Can a true believer fall into these sins? Yes, and Scripture records it: David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and the man in chapter 5 was a member of this church. But Paul is describing a way of life, not a single fall, and the believer who falls is brought back to repentance, as David was (Psalm 51). What cannot be true of someone born of God is that he goes on in these things, unrepentant, to the end (1 John 3:9–10). The warning is real, and it is one of the means God uses to keep his people from that road. The God who keeps his own to the end keeps them through warnings like this one, not in spite of them.

How should I treat a gay friend or family member? With the same love and honesty you would show anyone on this list, which includes you. Keep the friendship, keep eating together, keep listening; Jesus was a friend of sinners, and so should you be. Do not make one sin the whole of the person or the first thing you talk about. Their greatest need, like yours, is Christ, not first a change of behaviour. If they ask what you believe, tell them gently and truthfully, including what you believe about your own sin and your own need of grace. And if a Christian friend confides that they experience same-sex attraction, count it an honour that they trusted you, keep their confidence, and walk with them.

In a sentence. Or do you not know that wrongdoers will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral nor idolaters nor adulterers nor men who have sex with men nor thieves nor the greedy nor drunkards nor slanderers nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Do not deceive yourself. If a sin on this list rules your life, run to Christ today. He washes, sanctifies and justifies. And read the list slowly, looking for yourself and not for others. Greed is on it. Drunkenness is on it. Verbal abuse is on it. Ask which item you have quietly made peace with because your church never mentions it, and bring that one to the Lord first.

For worship. The kingdom from which the unrighteous are shut out is the kingdom of a holy God, and it is holy all the way through. No greed will spoil it, no lie will be told in it, no one will be cheated or abused or used there. It is the home every wounded heart has longed for. And the astonishing thing is not that the unrighteous are excluded, but that anyone is admitted. The King has opened his kingdom to former thieves and drunkards and adulterers, because his own Son was counted among the unrighteous for them, and he gives his inheritance as a gift to those who were disinherited.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the two Greek terms behind “men who practice homosexuality” refer to the passive and active partners in homosexual acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

And such were some of you. Four words in the Greek, and they change the temperature of the whole chapter. Paul has just written the most severe list in the letter, and his next sentence is that it describes the people he is writing to. Not people outside. Not a warning about the sort of person one might meet in Corinth. Some of you. The congregation contained former idolaters, former drunkards, former thieves, former practising homosexuals, men who had lived what verse 9 describes. That is who was sitting in the room when this letter was read aloud. And the tense is the gospel. Such were: past, finished, no longer the case. Paul does not write: such are some of you, but you are forgiven. He says the description has stopped being true. That is who they were. It is no longer who they are.

But you were washed. Then three verbs, and every one of them describes something done to them. “Washed” is apolouō, washed clean: cleansed from sin’s filth. It is probably a reference to the new birth, of which baptism is the sign (Titus 3:5; Acts 22:16). This is the answer to what sin leaves behind after the guilt is dealt with: the sense of being soiled, of carrying something that will not come off. A man may believe he is forgiven and still feel unclean, and this word is aimed at exactly that.

You were sanctified. Set apart as holy to God, transferred into his own possession: definitive sanctification. God claimed them as his own. Note that this is stated as an accomplished fact, not a target. It is the same thing Paul said in his opening greeting, addressing this troubled church as those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints (1:2). The daily work of growing in holiness follows, but it grows out of this: they already belong to God.

You were justified. Declared righteous before God: the legal word. Their guilt removed, the charge dismissed, Christ’s righteousness counted to them, standing before God as people against whom nothing can be brought (Romans 5:1; 8:33). Notice the order, because it is not the order a theologian would choose. Logically justification comes first: God declares, and then transforms. Paul puts sanctification before it. He is not listing these in logical order; all three happen together at conversion. He seems to move from what is most felt to what is most decisive: from the dirt coming off, to belonging to God, to the verdict that settles everything.

In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. All of it through Christ’s work and the Spirit’s application. Notice the Trinity: the Lord Jesus, the Spirit, our God the Father. The Son’s name, the Spirit’s power and the Father’s ownership, all in one clause. Nothing here was self-administered.

The verse for the person carrying a past. This is the verse for the reader who is carrying a past. Not a vague sense of having been imperfect, but something specific: the years you do not talk about, the thing you did that you cannot imagine saying out loud in a church, the pattern you were in before Christ found you, which surfaces at three in the morning to tell you what you really are. Paul’s answer is not that it was not serious. He has just spent two verses saying how serious it was. His answer is that it is in the past tense, that three things have happened to you since, and that not one of them depends on your assessment of yourself. Look at what the accusation always does: it uses the true past to establish a false present. This is what you are. And the reply is not a denial of the history but a statement about the tense. Such were some of you. You were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that former temptations will never return. But a believer’s identity is no longer defined by past sins or present temptations. You are washed, sanctified, justified.

Does “such were some of you” mean that the old desires disappear? Paul is describing a changed standing and a changed direction: these people are washed, set apart and declared righteous, and those sins are no longer who they are. He does not promise that temptation ends. Some believers find old desires greatly weakened; many, including those who experience same-sex attraction, go on being tempted and go on fighting, and that fight is the normal Christian life (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:17), not evidence that the gospel has failed. And “you were washed” points to the cleansing of the new birth (Titus 3:5), which baptism pictures (Acts 22:16) but does not itself accomplish.

Should a church welcome people with pasts like these? Yes, with open arms, because the church at Corinth was made of them. A church that is shocked by former thieves, addicts, adulterers or people who have lived a gay life has forgotten what it is. Every member is a former something. Welcome does not mean pretending sin does not matter; it means telling the truth Paul tells here, that Christ washes and changes sinners, and then walking with people as he changes them. If your church would struggle to welcome a person with a story like those in verse 9, ask what that says about how you understand your own story.

In a sentence. And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.

On a Tuesday. When your past speaks to you in the present tense, answer it in Paul’s tenses. Say it aloud if you need to: I was that; I was washed; I was sanctified; I was justified. Then live today as someone who has been washed, not as someone trying to get clean. And when you meet someone whose past is still their present, remember that you were once there, and that the same three verbs are on offer to them.

For worship. The washing was not a rinse, and the price is named at the end of this chapter. He did not tidy up the guilty; he bought them. The list in verse 9 is an accurate description of what he purchased, and he paid for it knowing every item, and he has never once suggested he overpaid. The Father chose, the Son shed his blood, the Spirit applied it, and a congregation of former idolaters and thieves became saints. Such were some of us. But we were washed, and the water was his blood, and the God who washed us will never call us dirty again (Titus 3:3–7; Romans 8:33–34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes up slogans the Corinthians were using. “Everything is permitted for me”, they said; yes, but not everything is helpful, and Paul will not be mastered by anything. “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food”, they said, meaning that the body’s appetites, including sex, do not matter; God will do away with both. But the body is not meant for sexual immorality. It is meant for the Lord, and the Lord for the body, and God, who raised the Lord, will raise us too. Believers’ bodies are members of Christ; should they unite them with a prostitute? Never. Whoever joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her, for Scripture says the two become one flesh, but whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him. So they must flee sexual immorality. Other sins are outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Their body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, who lives in them, given by God. They do not belong to themselves; they were bought at a price, so they must honour God with their bodies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul’s argument for sexual ethics is grounded in resurrection theology: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The body is not a temporary shell to be discarded but the vehicle of the self that God will raise — the same body, transformed. This is why what we do with the body matters eternally. The body-soul dualism that dismisses bodily sins as theologically insignificant — a common Gnostic error in the ancient world — is precisely what Paul is refuting. The resurrection of the body is the theological foundation of a robust, embodied Christian ethics.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a prostitute in Corinth was a normal feature of social life — not perceived as transgression but as participation in the city’s religious and social fabric. The Corinthian with a “strong” theology might have regarded it as religiously meaningless (the idol is nothing) and biologically natural. Paul’s counter-argument changes the frame entirely: it is not religiously meaningless because the Holy Spirit inhabits the believer’s body; the body is not yours to give away because it was bought with a price. Now: The sexual ethics of any age are shaped by whatever account it gives of the body. Paul’s account — the body as Spirit-indwelt, resurrection-destined, cross-purchased — is the most exalted account of human physicality in any worldview.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything.

All things are lawful for me. These words are probably a slogan used at Corinth, and Paul is almost certainly quoting it. Perhaps they had twisted his own teaching on Christian freedom, freedom from the law as a way of earning God’s favour, into a licence to do anything, including sexual sin. Notice that he does not simply deny the slogan. He could have; instead he lets it stand and puts two limits round it, which is far more useful. Christian freedom is real, and Paul will not surrender the principle even when it is being abused. What he refuses is the idea that freedom is the only question worth asking.

But not all things are helpful. The first limit. The word is sympherei, from sympherō: what is beneficial, profitable, what builds up. A thing may be entirely permitted and still be a bad idea. The question is not only, is it allowed? but, is it good for me and for others? That distinction is missing from a great deal of Christian decision-making, which tends to stop as soon as the question “is it forbidden?” has been answered. And notice what it does to the shape of the question. Is this allowed? is the question of a man looking for the edge of the territory he can occupy without penalty. Is this helpful? is the question of a man who wants to get somewhere. The first is the question of a servant checking the rules; the second is the question of a son who shares his father’s aim.

But I will not be dominated by anything. The second limit is the more penetrating. The Greek carries a wordplay the English cannot quite hold. The slogan says all things are exestin, permitted, within my authority. Paul replies that he will not be exousiasthēsomai, brought under the authority of, anything. Same root, turned round: I have authority to do all things, but I will not let anything have authority over me. Freedom that leads to slavery is not freedom. Many things that are permissible become addictions. And this exposes the irony in the Corinthian position with great precision. They were using the language of freedom to justify appetites that had them by the throat. A man who insists he is free to do a thing, and cannot stop doing it, is not describing liberty. He has simply found a theological vocabulary for his slavery.

How the pattern looks now. The pattern outlives its first setting. It is the drinker who is emphatic about Christian liberty in the matter of alcohol. The man who defends his viewing habits on the grounds that legalism is a greater danger. The person whose spending, or phone, or ambition is plainly running him, and who has an argument ready for anyone who raises it. In every case the giveaway is not the argument but the defensiveness, because a genuinely free man does not need to justify anything at length. He can simply stop.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul believed literally everything is lawful. He has just listed sins that exclude from the kingdom. The slogan applies at most to things God has left free.

What are the things God has left free? They are the many matters Scripture neither commands nor forbids: what you eat and drink in moderation, how you spend your leisure, what music you enjoy, which job you take, whether you own a television. Older writers called them things indifferent. In these, you have real freedom, and other Christians must not bind your conscience with rules God has not given (Romans 14:1–4; Colossians 2:20–23). But even here Paul gives you three questions to ask: is it helpful, to me and to others? Is it mastering me? And, as he will add later, does it glorify God (10:31)? Freedom is a gift to be used for Christ, not a fence to see how close you can stand to the edge.

In a sentence. “I have the right to do anything,” you say, but not everything is beneficial. “I have the right to do anything,” but Paul will not be mastered by anything.

On a Tuesday. Is there something permitted that has started to master you: your phone, food, entertainment, alcohol? Freedom means being able to say no. Here is the most practical test in the chapter. Take whatever you would defend on the grounds of Christian freedom, and do not argue about whether it is permitted. Put it down for a month. What happens next is the answer. If it goes without much difficulty, the freedom was real and you have lost nothing. If you find yourself negotiating, rationalising, or unable to face the month at all, then you have discovered which way the authority is running, and you were never arguing about liberty in the first place (Galatians 5:13; 2 Peter 2:19).

For worship. The freedom Christ gives is not the freedom to be ruled by our appetites but freedom from their rule. He came to proclaim liberty to the captives, and he broke the chains of sin by being bound for us. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36). And the only master he puts in place of our old masters is himself, the one Lord under whom his servants are most fully free, whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.
verseByVerse.note: The words in quotation marks are probably slogans used at Corinth, which Paul quotes and then corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”—and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food. Another slogan, and this one is an argument. The reasoning behind it is easy to reconstruct, and it is still in use. The body has appetites. Appetites exist to be satisfied. Hunger is met with food and nobody considers it a moral event; therefore sexual desire may be met wherever it is convenient, and it is no more significant than a meal. Eat when hungry; have sex when you desire it. Many Greeks thought the body was unimportant compared to the soul, and the Corinthian who visited a prostitute was not, on this account, doing anything of consequence: merely attending to a biological function.

And God will destroy both one and the other. Possibly also part of the slogan: the body will perish anyway, so what we do with it does not matter. Paul’s reply comes in two moves, and the first is to grant the analogy and show where it goes. Yes, food and the stomach belong to an order that is passing away. Digestion is a temporary arrangement. If you want to argue from what is passing, then admit that the whole category you are appealing to is on its way out. Paul agrees that food and stomach are temporary, but rejects the conclusion.

The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord. Then the reply proper, and it is one of the most remarkable sentences Paul ever wrote about the human body. The body (sōma) is not like the stomach. It is not one organ among many but the whole person in bodily existence, and it belongs to the Lord. Sexual immorality is not just an appetite; it involves the whole person.

And the Lord for the body. A stunning statement. Read it again. Not merely that the body is for the Lord, which we might have guessed, but that the Lord is for the body. God is committed to your physical self. He is not tolerating it, waiting for the real you to be released from it at death. He made it, he took one himself, he redeemed it, and he intends to raise it. That demolishes the slogan at the root. The Corinthian argument assumed the body was a machine with requirements. Paul says the body is a person, and the person belongs to Christ.

A doctrine of the body. And it is worth seeing how completely this cuts across the instinct of the ancient world, which held that the material was inferior and the spiritual was what mattered, so that what a man did with his body was either unimportant or a distraction from higher things. Christianity has never taught that, though Christians have often absorbed it. The faith whose central claims are an incarnation, a bodily resurrection and a coming new creation cannot regard flesh as an embarrassment. That is why sexual ethics in the New Testament are never presented as a set of arbitrary restrictions. They follow from a doctrine of the body so high that no other worldview comes near it. You will not find a rival account, ancient or modern, that says more about your physical self than that God became one, died in one, rose in one, and intends to give you one that will not decay.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body is evil or that food is wrong. It means the body is precious to God and must be used for his purposes.

Does God care about my sleep, my health and how I treat my body? Yes, though not in the way our culture worships the body. If the Lord is for the body, then what you do with yours is never spiritually neutral: not the sleep you refuse it, not the way you speak about it, not the contempt some Christians carry for their own physical selves and mistake for humility. Rest is a gift (Psalm 127:2), and bodily training is of some value (1 Timothy 4:8). But the body is not an idol to be perfected; it is a servant to be cared for and offered to God (Romans 12:1). Look after it as you would look after something precious lent to you by a friend.

Will we have bodies in eternity? Yes. When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with Christ, conscious and at rest, while his body waits in the grave (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). At Christ’s return the body will be raised, the same body and yet transformed, made imperishable and glorious like Christ’s own (15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). We will not float as spirits for ever. We will live, body and soul, on a renewed earth. That is why the body matters now: it is not a husk to be thrown away but the seed of what will be raised.

In a sentence. You say, “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy them both.” The body, however, is not meant for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week how you think about your body: as a machine to be fed, an enemy to be fought, an image to be managed, or a gift belonging to the Lord. Then do one concrete thing that treats it as his: go to bed at a reasonable hour, refuse something that harms it, use your hands to serve someone. He is for it. That is a stranger and kinder claim than most of us have let it be.

For worship. The Lord is for the body. The eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us; he was born with a body, hungered and thirsted in a body, was nailed to a cross in a body, and rose again in a body that the disciples could touch. He ascended in that body, and a man with scars in his hands is seated at the right hand of the Father. He will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). The God who made dust into Adam will not abandon the dust of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!

And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Paul is still answering the food-and-stomach argument, and he answers it with the resurrection. The logic runs like this. If the body were merely a temporary container, what is done with it would matter no more than what is done with a coat. But the body has a future. The body is not destroyed at death for good. The same power that brought Jesus out of the tomb is going to be applied to your physical self, and what will stand in the new creation is not a disembodied spirit but a raised person (15:20–23). So the body you are currently deciding what to do with is the body that will be there. What will be raised matters now. That is why chapter 15 is so important to the whole letter.

Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Then the second argument, moving from the future to the present. Members (melē) is the ordinary word for limbs and organs. This is not a metaphor about belonging to a club. Paul means that by union with Christ, the believer’s physical self is joined to him as a hand is joined to a body. Believers are united to Christ, body and soul. Your hands, eyes and whole body are parts of Christ.

Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Having said that, he draws the conclusion with deliberate bluntness. Prostitution was common in Corinth, sometimes connected with temples, and banquets and festivals often ended with it. To have sex with a prostitute is to take what belongs to Christ and join it to her. It is meant to shock, and it should. Paul refuses to let the sin be pictured privately, as a transaction between two consenting people in a room. He insists that Christ is not absent from it. The Christian does not leave his union with the Lord at the door and pick it up on the way out; there is no such door. Whatever a believer does with his body, he does as a limb of Christ.

Never! Mē genoito: absolutely not, the strongest negative in Paul’s vocabulary, the expression he reserves for a suggestion so appalling it does not deserve an argument. Unthinkable.

The modern form. The ancient application was the brothel, and the modern reader is inclined to file that under practices we no longer face. It would be a mistake. Paul’s argument is not about a particular institution; it is about what a body is. And the modern form of the same transaction, a screen, an image, another human being reduced to a function, entirely private and entirely deniable, is available to almost every reader of this page, at any hour, at no cost and with no witnesses. Every defence of that habit depends on its being nobody else’s business: it harms no one, nothing is happening, it is only an image. Paul’s answer is that something is happening, and that the Lord is present at it, because the man doing it is a limb of Christ and does not stop being one for the duration. And the image on the screen is a person too, often exploited, sometimes trafficked, made in God’s image and used as a product.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who falls into sexual sin is no longer joined to Christ. It shows the horror and contradiction of such sin.

If I have fallen into this, has Christ let go of me? No. That is precisely why it matters so much what you take him into: he does not withdraw when you sin. That is a heavier thought than shame, and it is also more hopeful, because shame merely tells a man what he is and leaves him there. This tells him whose he is. The argument for purity here is not that you are dirty and must clean yourself up. It is that you are joined to Christ, already, now, in the body. So come back to him at once, confess it plainly (1 John 1:9), bring it into the light with a trusted believer, and take practical steps against it. His hold on you is the ground of your fight, not the prize for winning it.

In a sentence. By his power God raised the Lord from the dead, and he will raise us also. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ himself? Shall Paul then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never!

On a Tuesday. Your body is a part of Christ. Do not take it anywhere, or do anything with it, that you would not take Christ to. Before you open the app, enter the room or click the link, ask the plain question: am I about to take a limb of Christ here? And then use those same limbs for him today: hands that help, eyes that look on others with honour, feet that go where love sends them (Romans 6:12–13; 12:27).

For worship. God raised the Lord, and God will raise us. The power that rolled away the stone and brought the crucified body of Jesus out alive is the power at work in every believer, and it will one day reach into every grave where his people lie. And between his resurrection and ours, he has joined our bodies to himself. The risen Christ does not hold his people at arm’s length. He has made them his own limbs, and he will not lose a single one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.

Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? Paul now explains why the food analogy fails, and he does it by quoting Genesis about a prostitute. “Joined” is kollaō, glued, cleaved to. Sex is never merely physical. It unites two persons. Even a casual encounter creates a real union.

For, as it is written, the two will become one flesh. The citation is Genesis 2:24, the wedding verse, the charter of marriage, spoken in Eden before the fall. God designed sexual union to express and seal the lifelong covenant union of husband and wife (Matthew 19:5–6). And Paul applies it to a paid encounter with a stranger. That is the whole argument, and it is devastating. The Corinthian position was that this sort of thing carries no weight: a transaction, a bodily function, nothing exchanged but money. Paul says the one-flesh bond forms regardless. It was built into the act by God at creation, and it does not wait to be authorised by the intentions of the people involved. Neither of them meant a union. A union occurred. Used outside marriage, it still creates a union, but a false and destructive one.

Why casual sex is not casual. This is why sex can never be what every generation keeps insisting it can be: a thing done with the body alone, walked away from, filed under recreation. Paul’s claim is not merely that casual sex is emotionally unwise, though it is. It is that there is no such thing: the act is a covenant-shaped act whether or not a covenant exists, and doing it outside one does not neutralise it but tears it. And experience is not against him. People discover, repeatedly and to their own surprise, that they cannot dispose of these attachments as easily as the theory promised; that someone they were assured meant nothing turns out to be lodged in them years later. Paul told us why. Something was joined that was designed not to come apart.

But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him. Then the sentence the whole argument has been building to. Paul uses the same verb both times, kollaō, to be glued, cemented. He deliberately sets the two unions side by side in identical language, and the effect is to make them mutually intolerable: not merely unwise together, but contradictory. The man is already joined to Christ. He is proposing to be joined to somebody else. Believers are united to Christ in a spiritual union, by the Spirit, which is even deeper than marriage, the reality to which marriage itself points (Ephesians 5:31–32). Sexual immorality sets up a rival union.

A rival intimacy, and a greater one. Here the passage turns from prohibition to something better. Paul’s final answer to sexual sin is not a rule. It is a rival intimacy, and a greater one. The believer is one spirit with the Lord: a union closer than the one being contemplated, permanent where that is momentary, and satisfying at a depth the other cannot reach even when it delivers everything it promises. That is worth saying plainly to anyone fighting here, because the fight is usually lost at the level of desire rather than of information. Nobody has ever been kept pure merely by being told that sex is serious; they knew. What holds is knowing what you already have. Purity that is only refusal is a starvation diet, and starvation diets do not last. The Christian is not being asked to want less. He is being asked to notice that he is already joined to Someone, and to want that more, which is the only appetite strong enough to displace the other one (Psalm 63:1–5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a sexual encounter creates a marriage. It means sex has a meaning that cannot be emptied out, which is why it belongs in marriage.

I have a sexual past. Am I bound for ever to the people I slept with? No. The union Paul describes is real, and its wounds can be real, but it is not a marriage and it does not own you. Christ’s union with you is stronger, and his blood washes every sin of the past (v. 11). Confess it to God, receive his forgiveness as fully as he gives it, and ask him to heal the memories and attachments that remain; often it helps to talk with a wise pastor or counsellor. Many believers with painful sexual histories go on to know deep joy in Christ, and in a faithful marriage. The past is real, but it is not the strongest bond in your life.

What if I was sexually abused? Then you did not sin; you were sinned against. Paul is speaking here about what people choose to do with their bodies, not what was done to them by force or manipulation. Nothing done to you without your free consent has joined you to your abuser in the sense of this verse, and none of the guilt is yours. Your body remains a member of Christ and a temple of his Spirit, and he is not ashamed of you. Please tell someone safe, seek help, and, where a crime has been committed, report it. Christ, who was himself stripped and shamed by cruel men, stands with the wounded, and he promises to bind up the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3).

In a sentence. Do you not know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, “The two will become one flesh.” But whoever is united with the Lord is one with him in spirit.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes, do not only remind yourself of the rule; remind yourself of the union. Turn the moment into prayer to the One you are already joined to, and ask him for a greater taste of his love than the thing in front of you offers. If you are married, give yourself gladly to your spouse, because marriage is the God-given home of this union (7:3–5). If you are single, know that you are not missing the deepest union there is; you already have it.

For worship. You are joined to the Lord, one spirit with him. The Bridegroom has bound himself to his people with a bond that no sin can dissolve and no death can break. He gave himself up for his bride, to sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word (Ephesians 5:25–26). Every earthly union, even the best marriage, is a picture of this one, and the picture will pass when the reality comes. One day the marriage supper of the Lamb will be spread, and the bride will see the face of the one she has been joined to all along.

parallels.desc: they shall become one flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.

Flee from sexual immorality. One word, and it is the whole strategy. “Flee” is pheugō: run away from. And the tense is continuous: keep fleeing, make it a habit rather than an emergency measure. Not argue with it, flirt with it, or test your strength against it, but run. This is not how the New Testament speaks about most temptation. Elsewhere Christians are told to stand, to resist the devil, to put on armour and hold their ground (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:13). Here the instruction is the opposite, and the change is deliberate. In this particular fight, standing your ground to prove you can is not courage. It is how people lose. The model is Joseph, and the detail in Genesis is exact. He does not debate with Potiphar’s wife, or reason with her, or test how much of the conversation he can survive. He runs out of the house and leaves his garment in her hand (Genesis 39:12; 2 Timothy 2:22). It cost him his reputation and his liberty, and it was the right decision.

Every other sin a person commits is outside the body. The clause is genuinely difficult, and commentators divide over it. Some think Paul is again quoting a Corinthian saying, every sin is outside the body, and then contradicting it. Others take it as Paul’s own statement, meaning that sexual sin is unique in its relation to the body.

But the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Of the two readings, the second is the more likely. Drunkenness and gluttony also harm the body, but they act on it from outside. In sexual sin the body itself is given to another and the two become one flesh (v. 16), so the sin is committed with the very body that is joined to the Lord (vv. 15, 17). It is the one act in which the body is the instrument, the currency and the thing given away. It is not that it is the worst sin, but that it involves giving one’s own body to another in a union meant only for marriage. It defiles the body that is the Lord’s and the Spirit’s temple, and the damage lands on the person committing it.

What fleeing looks like. The command is useless if it stays abstract, and the modern form of this battle is often a device in a pocket. Fleeing is not what most people attempt. What most people attempt is resisting at the point of temptation, using willpower, at the exact moment when willpower is least available: late, tired, alone, discouraged. That is a fight nobody wins for long, and the repeated failure then produces the despair that makes the next failure easier. Fleeing happens earlier, and it is structural rather than heroic. It means the decision is taken at ten in the morning, not eleven at night. It means the filter installed, the device out of the bedroom, the account handed to somebody else, the route home changed, the friendship that has begun to warm quietly cooled before anyone has said anything they cannot unsay. It is unglamorous and slightly humiliating, and that is a mark in its favour: a person willing to look foolish about this has understood what he is dealing with. And it means telling somebody. Sin that has to be reported to a friend on Thursday loses a great deal of its power on Wednesday.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sexual sin is unforgivable. It is washed away like every other sin (v. 11). Nor does it mean other sins (like drunkenness) have no bodily effects.

Does fleeing mean avoiding everyone of the opposite sex? No. Paul worked closely with women in the gospel (Romans 16:1–7; Philippians 4:2–3), and Jesus spoke alone with a Samaritan woman. Fleeing is not fear of people; it is wisdom about situations. It means knowing your own weaknesses and setting sensible boundaries: being careful about privacy and secrecy, about emotional intimacy with someone who is not your spouse, about the moments and places where you know you are vulnerable. Treat older women as mothers and younger women as sisters, in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). The aim is honour toward others, not suspicion of them.

What if I keep falling, even after I have tried to flee? Then do not stop fleeing, and do not stop coming back to Christ. Repeated failure tempts you to give up, either by concluding you can never change or by deciding it does not matter. Both are lies. Confess it honestly to God, who is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). Tell a mature Christian and let him help you see where the battle is actually being lost, which is usually earlier than you think. Strengthen the barriers, and ask for help if it has become an addiction. Many have walked out of long patterns of sin by God’s grace, often slowly. The Spirit who lives in you is stronger than the habit.

In a sentence. Flee from sexual immorality. All other sins a person commits are outside the body, but whoever sins sexually sins against their own body.

On a Tuesday. Plan your escape routes: what you will do, where you will go, whom you will call, when temptation comes. Then flee. And here is a simple test: name the last time you were in this fight, and identify the point at which it was actually decided. It will not have been the moment of failure. It will have been somewhere earlier and quieter, and that earlier point is where the word flee belongs (Proverbs 4:14–15).

For worship. The One who commands us to flee is the One who never had to flee from his own heart. Jesus was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and his purity was not cold or fearful but full of love and warmth toward the very people others used. Because he stood where we fall, there is a refuge to flee to as well as a danger to flee from. We run from sin into the arms of the Saviour, and he is a sympathetic High Priest who gives mercy and grace to help in time of need.

parallels.desc: Joseph fled

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you. Paul said something very like this three chapters ago, but there the pronouns were plural and the temple was the congregation (3:16). Here each believer’s body is in view. The church together is God’s temple, and so is the individual believer’s physical body. Both are true, and the second is the one this chapter needs. Temple is naos: not the whole complex of courts but the inner sanctuary, the place where God dwells. Consider what that meant in a city like Corinth, where temples were everywhere and everyone knew how they worked. A temple was the place a god was held to reside, and its holiness followed entirely from that residence. Nothing about the stone was special. What made a temple a temple was the occupant. So the argument is not that your body is impressive, or attractive, or in good order. It is that Someone lives there. The Holy Spirit lives in your body. Sexual sin brings the Holy One into the brothel.

Whom you have from God? The Spirit is God’s gift (2:12). You did not earn him. He is a gift, not an achievement, and therefore not something any believer can claim to be too unworthy to have received.

You are not your own. Five words that cut directly across the deepest assumption most people hold about themselves, then and now. It is the opposite of the modern slogan, my body, my choice. The believer does not own himself. Paul denies self-ownership flatly, and it is worth being honest that this is not a comfortable sentence; it is a claim of ownership over the one thing every human being reserves.

For you were bought with a price. But look at how he grounds it, because the ground changes everything. “Bought” is agorazō, the marketplace word, the language of the slave market. Somebody paid, and the payment transferred ownership. Paul does not name the sum here. He does not need to; this letter has been circling it since chapter 1. The price was the cross: not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19; Revelation 5:9). You belong to your new master, and he is a master who bought you to set you free. That is the answer to anyone who hears “you are not your own” as a threat to their freedom. You are owned by someone who bought you at his own cost, having assessed you accurately, and who has never once complained about the price. And it turns the sentence into the most reassuring in the chapter rather than the most confining. If you are not your own, then you are not finally at the mercy of your own failures, your own assessment of yourself, or your own capacity to hold on. The body you have treated badly, the self you are ashamed of, the life you suspect you have wasted: none of it is yours to write off, because none of it is yours.

So glorify God in your body. The conclusion. And notice that the chapter ends on a positive command rather than a prohibition. Paul has spent seven verses on what must be fled; he finishes with what the body is actually for. Use your body to show God’s worth: in purity, service, work, worship. Hands that work honestly, a tongue that tells the truth and blesses rather than reviles, a face that is glad to see people, feet that go where they are needed, arms that pick up a child, a body spent in service and eventually worn out in it: all of that is what this verse asks for, and none of it is possible for someone who thinks his body is either a machine or an embarrassment.

A textual note. Some later manuscripts add “and in your spirit, which are God’s”; the shorter reading is original. The addition is true, but Paul’s point in this chapter is deliberately about the body.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you must hate or neglect your body. It means you care for it and use it as God’s property, for his glory.

Does this verse forbid smoking, tattoos or unhealthy food? Its first meaning is narrower: Paul is writing about sexual immorality, and a body that belongs to the Lord must not be joined to a prostitute. But the principle reaches further, because the body is not ours. We are to care for it as belonging to God, and other texts plainly forbid drunkenness and gluttony (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:20–21). What the verse does not do is settle every question of habit or appearance; the ban on tattoos in Leviticus 19:28 belonged to Israel’s separation from pagan mourning rites. Where Scripture does not forbid, Paul’s own test from verse 12 applies: is it helpful, and am I being mastered by it?

If I am not my own, must I let others do what they like with my body? No; the very opposite. You are not your own because you belong to Christ, not because you belong to anyone else. No husband, wife, boyfriend, employer or church leader owns your body, and no one has the right to use, hurt or control it. Belonging to Christ is your protection. If someone is abusing or coercing you, it is right to say no, to get to safety and to seek help, including from the police. The Lord who bought you at the cost of his own blood is not indifferent to what is done to his temple, and he calls his church to protect the vulnerable, not to hand them back.

In a sentence. Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honour God with your bodies.

On a Tuesday. Begin tomorrow by offering your body to God before your feet touch the floor: Lord, I am not my own; you bought me with your blood. Then choose one ordinary way to glorify him in your body during the day: honest work with your hands, a kind word with your tongue, care for someone who is ill, rest you have been refusing. A temple is not only kept clean; it is used for worship (Romans 12:1).

For worship. The temple in Jerusalem was destroyed, and the God who had filled it did not become homeless. He moved into people: into a fractious congregation in a port city, and into the bodies of men and women who had been on the list in verse 9, washed, sanctified, justified, and now inhabited. He looked at what could be bought in that market, and he paid the full price without haggling, with the blood of his own Son, and he moved in. The Spirit of the living God has made his home in jars of clay, and he will not leave until he has raised them in glory. We are not our own. We are his, and there is no better place in all creation to belong (John 2:19–21).
verseByVerse.note: “Bought with a price” uses the language of the slave market.

7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
From chapter 7 Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The first concerns sex and marriage. Some in Corinth had swung to the opposite extreme from the immorality of chapter 6: they said it was better for a man not to touch a woman at all, even in marriage, and perhaps that believers should divorce unbelieving spouses or not marry. Roman society, by contrast, pressed people to marry: the emperor Augustus had passed laws penalising the unmarried. Paul steers between both pressures.

Married couples should not deny each other sexually, except briefly by agreement for prayer. Singleness is good and Paul himself prefers it, but it is a gift, and those without it should marry. Believers should not divorce, as Jesus taught; a believer married to an unbeliever should stay if the unbeliever is willing, but is not bound if the unbeliever leaves. In general, each person should serve God in the situation in which he was called, whether circumcised or not, slave or free, though a slave who can gain freedom should take it. Because the time is short and the world in its present form is passing away, and because of a present crisis, Paul advises the unmarried to consider staying single, so as to serve the Lord without divided concerns. But marriage is no sin, and a widow may remarry, only to a believer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the questions in their letter, beginning with the claim that it is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. Because sexual immorality is a real danger, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Husband and wife owe each other sexual intimacy; neither has sole rights over their own body, for each belongs to the other. They should not deprive each other except by mutual agreement for a limited time of prayer, and then come together again, so that Satan does not exploit their lack of self-control. Paul says this as a concession, not a command. He wishes everyone could be single as he is, but each person has his own gift from God. To the unmarried and widows he says it is good to stay single as he does, but if they cannot control themselves they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with desire.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

Reformed theology has always resisted the Catholic elevation of celibacy above marriage as the spiritually superior state. The Reformers read 1 Corinthians 7 as affirming both callings as genuine gifts of God, neither intrinsically superior. Luther’s own marriage was a theological act — a public demonstration that marriage is not a second-class spiritual status. Paul’s careful handling of both callings in vv. 7–9 supports this reading: celibacy is a charisma, a grace-gift, as is marriage. Neither is commanded; both are honoured.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics who were advocating celibacy within marriage may have been influenced by the same Gnostic-adjacent body-negativity that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6 — but in the opposite direction: if the body is spiritually inferior, why give it what it desires? Paul’s answer refuses both the libertine and the ascetic extremes. Now: The Christian tradition has tended to err in one direction or the other in every generation: either treating sexuality as a dangerous force to be suppressed, or (more recently) treating it as a sovereign identity that cannot be questioned. Paul’s account makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant obligation, eschatologically relativised.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 7 is the Bible’s longest discussion of marriage and singleness. Some in Corinth had swung the opposite way from the immorality of chapter 6: they thought sex itself was unspiritual, and that believers should abstain even in marriage, or leave their marriages altogether. Paul answers their questions one by one. Marriage is good, and sexual union within it is a mutual duty and gift; married couples should not deprive each other (vv. 1–7). Singleness is also good, and a gift, but those who burn with desire should marry (vv. 8–9). Married believers must not divorce; if one is married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay, the believer should stay; if the unbeliever leaves, the believer is not bound (vv. 10–16). In general, Christians should remain in the situation in which God called them, whether married or single, Jew or Gentile, slave or free, for what matters is keeping God’s commands (vv. 17–24). Finally, because the time is short and this world is passing away, singleness has real advantages for undivided devotion to the Lord; but marrying is no sin (vv. 25–40). The chapter honours both marriage and singleness as callings from God, and behind every line of it stands a Lord who assigns each of his people a life, calls them in it, and has never yet handed anybody the wrong one.

Now concerning the matters about which you wrote. With this sentence the whole shape of the letter changes. Until now Paul has been responding to reports that reached him from Chloe’s people (1:11) and to rumours about the church (5:1). From here he is answering a letter the Corinthians sent him, question by question, and the phrase “now concerning” (peri de) marks each new topic through the rest of the book: marriage (7:1), the betrothed (7:25), food offered to idols (8:1), spiritual gifts (12:1), the collection (16:1), and Apollos (16:12). It is worth pausing on the humility of that. The apostle does not set his own agenda and lecture a church on what he thinks it needs. He takes their questions seriously, in their order, and answers them as a pastor answers a letter from people he loves.

It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. Literally, not to touch a woman, a polite expression for sexual relations. And because Paul is now quoting their letter, this sentence is very probably their words, not his. The ESV puts it in quotation marks for that reason. It is the slogan of a party at Corinth, ascetics who were saying that even married couples should abstain, and Paul is about to spend forty verses qualifying it. Getting that right matters enormously, because the chapter has been badly misread for centuries by people who took the slogan as Paul’s own settled view. Read that way, this becomes the passage where the New Testament grudgingly concedes that marriage is permissible for those who cannot manage better, and a great deal of unhappy teaching about sex and the body has been built on it.

Two errors that are really one. What Paul does is more interesting than either agreeing or dismissing. He will grant that singleness has real advantages, and he will insist that the ascetics have no business imposing it on anyone. Remember the church he is writing to. Chapter 6 dealt with a party for whom the body did not matter because it was disposable: so do what you like with it. Here is a party for whom the body did not matter because it should be denied: so give it nothing. They look like opposites. They are the same error, a contempt for the body God made and Christ redeemed, and Paul refuses both. The body is for the Lord, and the Lord for the body (6:13), whether it is being kept from a prostitute or given to a husband.

But because of the temptation to sexual immorality. Literally, because of immoralities, plural: the many forms of it on every street of a port city like Corinth. Given the strength of sexual desire, enforced abstinence inside marriage would not produce saints. It would produce sin.

Each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. “Have” here probably means have sexual relations with, within marriage. And notice the form of the sentence: one wife, one husband, his own and her own, in perfect parallel. Monogamy, and complete mutuality, before Paul has even begun to argue. Marriage is God’s good provision for sexual desire, not a regrettable allowance for it. The answer is blunt and unromantic, and it is often quoted as though Paul thought marriage existed only to manage lust. He thought no such thing, and we should not read a specific answer as a complete doctrine. This is the apostle who wrote of a husband loving his wife as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25–32), and who grounded marriage in Genesis 2 rather than in the management of desire. Here he is answering one question from one church with one particular problem, and the answer is pitched at the problem.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the only reason to marry is to avoid sin. Scripture gives many purposes for marriage: companionship, for it is not good that the man should be alone (Genesis 2:18); children (Genesis 1:28); a living picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:32); and the prevention of immorality (Westminster 24.2). Paul is answering a specific question here, not writing a full theology of marriage.

Realism without shame. The blunt answer is also a kind one, and it is a mark of Scripture’s realism about people. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to aspire to a purity they will not sustain. He tells them, in effect: you are not made of iron, you live in Corinth, and God has provided for this. There is no shaming in it. That is a note to hold for the whole chapter, because it is unusually easy to read this material and come away condemned, married readers feeling second-rate and single readers feeling deficient. Paul’s tone is not that. He is a pastor answering a real letter from real people about how to live, and the strongest thing in his answer is not a standard but a refusal to bind anyone’s conscience where God has not (1 Timothy 4:1–5).

Is sexual desire itself sinful, then?
